articles.title: Rainfall supercharged by El Niño floods roads and collapses a south Florida synagogue's roof
articles.description: Rainfall supercharged by El Niño floods roads and collapses a south Florida synagogue's roof AP News Is more rain and flooding expected Thursday? What the forecast says Miami Herald Flood watch continues in South Florida, more flooding possible USA Today St. Johns River in Cocoa rises to record levels Spectrum News 13 Families rescued, neighborhoods underwater in Hollywood after historic flooding NBC 6 South Florida
articles.content: PLANTATION, Fla. (AP) — A slow-moving storm system dumped heavy rains in South Florida, flooding some streets and homes, closing sections of highways and collapsing the roof of a synagogue Wednesday. On the West Coast, heavy rain and high winds temporarily grounded planes at San Francisco’s airport, disrupted ferry service and flooded roads in Napa County and other wine country areas north of the city. Preliminary figures for Florida showed 15.3 inches (39 centimeters) of rain fell in a 24-hour period ending Wednesday in parts of Broward County, the National Weather Service said. The threat was expected to last through Friday along Florida’s Atlantic Coast with additional rainfall amounts of 12 inches (30 centimeters) possible, the weather service said. A low-pressure system is expected to form near the northern Bahamas. It could become a subtropical or tropical storm over parts of the southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts into early next week, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami. The natural warming cycle called El Niño has disrupted Florida’s typical dry season that runs from October to May, said Alejandra Garcia, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Miami. El Niño is “helping bring these low pressure systems down toward the southeastern United States, which in turn is causing these heavy precipitation events,” she said. In Florida, Broward County and the cities of Fort Lauderdale and Hollywood declared states of emergency. Hollywood Mayor Josh Levy urged people to avoid driving and unnecessary travel. Portions of the Florida Turnpike and Interstate 95 in Hollywood were closed due to high water and stalled vehicles. The city said it received more than 300 calls for service overnight. “It’s a historically significant rainfall event in the city,” Levy said. Some residents complained that drivers caused a wake that pushed floodwaters into their homes, he said. Heavy rains caused the roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood to collapse and damaged the roof and flooded hallways at a hospital. No injuries were reported. Rudy Taillard flew back from Texas on Tuesday night to find his apartment complex in the city flooded. “It was insane. The water kept going up,” Taillard said. “If you were living on the first floor, like, you were cooked. It was pretty brutal. Thank God I’m on the top floor.” The highest rainfall amount was recorded in Plantation, where resident Jade Jaime said the storm just kept going all day “and then by the time we went to sleep at night, still just pouring down like it was never going to end.” In Fort Lauderdale, the 5.72 inches (14.5 centimeters) of rain that fell in a downpour ending early Wednesday broke the daily record of 1.8 inches (4.5 centimeters) set in 1959, Garcia said. Officials announced that schools will be closed Thursday in Broward and Miami-Dade counties. In northern Florida, a warning was issued for minor flooding along the St. Johns River. The Los Angeles County Fire Department issued an evacuation warning through Friday morning for the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn scar areas, warning of a risk of debris flows as a storm approaches. South of San Francisco, a 47-mile (76-kilometer) segment of Highway 1 near Big Sur was closed Wednesday for the same reason. In San Francisco, which set a daily record with 2.28 inches (5.8 centimeters) of rain, the fire department responded to more than 300 calls Wednesday morning, many of which were related to flooding, along with downed trees and electrical wires, Chief Dean Crispen said during a news conference. By Wednesday night, some San Francisco flights were delayed hours because of wind. Areas along the Embarcadero were flooded as waves crashed over barricades recently installed to prevent flooding near the Ferry Building, a waterfront landmark. Officials canceled several ferries leading from the city due to the storm. Several highways were blocked by flooding or debris in Napa, Marin, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties, according to the California Department of Transportation and the California Highway Patrol. Northeast of San Francisco, flooding forced the evacuation of a school in Antioch, according to police and fire officials. Gusts up to 50 mph (80 kph) were forecast for the East Bay region and up to 70 mph (113 kph) for the Altamont Pass, which connects Bay Area highways to I-5 in the Central Valley. Snow accumulations of up to 4 feet (1.2 meters) were forecast through Friday in the highest portions of the Sierra Nevada. The weather service issued a long-range forecast showing heavy rain is possible along the Atlantic seaboard in Georgia and South Carolina on Saturday, from North Carolina to New York’s Long Island on Sunday and into New England on Sunday and Monday. Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. Associated Press writers Olga R. Rodriguez in San Francisco, Hallie Golden in Seattle and videojournalist Daniel Kozin in Hollywood, Florida, contributed.

Battle of unbeatens Romeo, Cass Tech highlight area semifinals
articles.content: Romeo is the sole prep football program still remaining in the MHSAA state tournament. Plus there are two other fringe schools from the Macomb Area Conference and Blue Water Area Conference that are still entertaining state championship dreams – Almont and Grosse Pointe South, which are just over the Macomb County boarders in Lapeer and Wayne counties. In the 11-man state tournament, there are eight divisions and only 32 schools still practicing and preparing these days. There will be some prayers answered this weekend – all state semifinals games across the state will be played Saturday afternoon – and also some dreams dashed. It’s Final Four time in the MHSAA state tournament. Below is a breakdown of each eastside game: DETROIT CASS TECH (12-0) VS. ROMEO (12-0) AT TROY ATHENS: Prep football fans have what they wanted. Three of the four state semifinalist teams in Division 1 are 12-0 at this stage and the fourth school is 11-1. Could a fan ask for anything more? These two teams have been perfect and all indications are that this could be a classic battle with a berth in the state title game on the line. Romeo, which won the Division 1 state title in 2015, is 12-0 for the first time in school history. The Macomb Area Conference Red Division champion Bulldogs have outscored the opposition 496-172 and have played a challenging schedule. Still, Romeo has averaged 41.3 points a game while giving up only 14.3 points per outing with one shutout. Cass Tech, which has won D-1 state titles in 2011, 2012, 2014 and 2024, has also put together some incredible numbers. The Technicians, the Detroit PSL Blue Division champs, have outscored the opposition 534-112 and averaged 44.5 points a game while allowing just 9.3 points an outing. Both teams also have several players that will suit up at various levels of the college football spectrum. Again, this game could be an epic battle – the kind of game that fans expect at this level of the state’s large-school division. ALMONT (12-0) VS. KINGSLEY (12-0) AT CLARE: Coming off four straight Blue Water Area Conference championships, Almont took down previously unbeaten powerhouse Marine City (41-14) last Friday and now must face another unbeaten team in the semifinals in Kingsley, which won the Northern Shores Conference this season. Both of these schools have been impressive in recent years. Almont’s resume includes six tripos to the Final Four, including in both 2025 and 2026, and are 2-3 all-time in state semifinals contests. The Raiders lost in the state finals in 2019 and 2023. Last year, Almont dropped a heartbreaker amongst heartbreaker with a 25-19 loss to eventual champion Jackson Lumen Christi in a game that reached triple overtime. Kingsley is making its fifth appearance in the state semifinals in the past 21 seasons, including 2005, 2019, 2023, 2025 and 2026. These two schools met only once – and that was on the big stage – during the 2023 Division 6 state finals. The Stags defeated Almont 38-24. Both teams have put up some gaudy numbers this season. Almont has outscored the opposition 481-198, averaging 42.0 points per game while giving up 16.5 a contest all while playing a pretty tough schedule. Kingsley has a 514-171 scoring edge which is an impressive 42.8 points an outing and only 4.3 points a game. These two programs have morphed into state powerhouse status and the winner will have to earn their berth into the state finals. ORCHARD LAKE ST. MARY’S (9-3) VS. GROSSE POINTE SOUTH (11-1) AT NOVI: For just the second time, Grosse Pointe South is playing in the state semifinals with one of its most talented overall rosters in program history. The Blue Devils have a future NCAA Division I quarterback and several other players that could end up at NCAA Division I and Division II schools and their only loss was by two points to Division 1 state semifinalist Romeo (28-26). St. Mary’s has made countless Final Four runs and also has a bevy of D-I and D-II athletes. The Eaglets play in the challenging CHSL Central Division while Grosse Pointe South comes from the Macomb Area Conference Red Division. Historically, these two conferences are also two of the best in the state in football and each league has two teams playing in the MHSAA Final Four. St. Mary’s has a 492-206 scoring edge, averaging 41.0 points per game offensively while holding the opposition down to 17.2 points per game. Grosse Pointe South has outscored the opposition 512-125, conceding only 10.4 points per game while scoring 42.7. Whichever team plays the best defense or has the ball the best may win this game.

Appeals court finds Michigan abortion restrictions unconstitutional under voter-approved amendment
articles.description: The ruling throws out a 24-hour mandatory waiting period for an abortion, required informed consent forms, and a ban on advanced clinicians like midwives or nurse practitioners performing an abortion.
articles.content: (Jodi Westrick / Michigan Public )The Michigan Court of Appeals says a statewide abortion rights referendum has invalidated restrictions that remain in state law.At issue were three provisions on the books before the amendment was ratified by voters: a 24-hour mandatory waiting period for an abortion; required informed consent forms; and a ban on advanced clinicians like midwives or nurse practitioners performing an abortion.In the unanimous ruling, the justices said those provisions were incompatible with the Reproductive Freedom For All amendment and therefore unconstitutional.Genevieve Marnon, the legislative director for Right to Life of Michigan, said the group isn’t involved in the lawsuit. However, they are keeping an eye on it.“We want them to have physicians providing their late-term abortions or second-trimester abortions,” Marnon said.In a statement, Planned Parenthood of Michigan President and CEO Paula Thornton Greear applauded the ruling, saying “These laws had nothing to do with patient health.”Thornton Greear said the state Legislature should remove the restrictions completely now that the appeals court has said they’re unconstitutional.“Even with this ruling, the laws are still written into Michigan statute, and when the new Legislature convenes in January, it’s time to take them off the books and enact new legislation to enforce the state constitution and protect the rights of patients and providers,” Thornton Greear said.Marnon cautioned lawmakers to not go too far.“For example, the parental consent law,” Marnon said. “I think if lawmakers decide that they're going to circumvent parents' rights, they may find a lot of parents that are not happy about that.”

articles.title: Advocates want tighter rules for who can be on the Michigan Sentencing Commission
articles.description: State law requires the sentencing commission to include at least one formerly incarcerated person. That spot is now held by a Republican former state Senator who spent one night in jail, suspected of drunk driving earlier this year.
articles.content: (Michigan Legislative Council Legislative Corrections Ombudsman)A new bill in the Michigan House of Representatives would add more requirements to serving on the Michigan Sentencing Commission.The 15-member panel is responsible for recommending sentencing guidelines. It’s supposed to include someone who was “previously incarcerated.”Justice advocates, however, want that language tightened to specify that the person needs to have spent at least five years in state prison.Jose Burgos is a former juvenile lifer who now works on sentencing reforms. He said “a night in jail” doesn’t make someone an expert on sentencing.“Those of us who have been impacted by the system not only understand the implications ... that the sentencing guidelines has on thousands of residents in the state of Michigan. But we also know the process of reentry, we also know the impact that this has on families, the impact that this has on communities,” Burgos said during a press conference Wednesday.Lawmakers resurrected the Michigan Sentencing Commission with a 2024 law.At the time, supporters reasoned punishments needed updating, since Michigan inmates are serving some of the longest minimum sentences in the country. Meanwhile, Michigan’s public safety ratings didn’t correspond with the punishment lengths.Earlier versions of the legislation had the senate majority leader and house speaker jointly picking who would represent formerly incarcerated people on the commission. The commission chair would have picked a candidate from each person’s preference, or on their own if the two leaders couldn’t agree.The final version, however, let either the Senate majority leader or minority leader pick that representative on their own.Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt (R-Porter Township) picked former state Sen. Rick Jones, who was arrested for suspected drunk driving in February. Jones spent one night in jail and received six months’ probation, according to court records.Kenneth Nixon, with the group Safe and Just Michigan, said it’s “heartbreaking” to see the spot go to someone who can’t speak to the things people who spent time in prison experienced.“Difficulties associated with being unable to communicate with family or raise your kids or be a part of the growth of other people, being able to support each other now on the outside because of your lived experience: He can’t have a conversation with us about those things,” Nixon said.Other speakers at Wednesday’s press conference questioned whose voice wouldn’t be heard because of Jones holding the seat.State Rep. Kara Hope (D-Holt) worked on the original bills and now sponsors the ones to update the policy. She said it should have been obvious that spending a short time in county jail didn’t equal actual incarcerated experience.“Power can be misused sometimes, and I think that’s what we saw here — misused to shut out the very people that we meant to give a seat at the table,” Hope saidSenate Republican communications staff did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday.Hope said she didn’t expect her bill to come up for a vote in the Michigan Legislature before the end of the term this year. But she said state Rep. Stephanie Young (D-Detroit), who will continue to serve as Democratic House caucus chair, pledged to take the issue back up next term, when her party controls both the House and Senate.

Arizona says it is investigating OpenAI, other firms over possible rogue agents
articles.content: CHICAGO, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The state of Arizona has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies relating to the "apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents," Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said Wednesday. A criminal investigation does not necessarily mean charges will be brought. Mayes said her office was investigating whether Arizona state law was being violated on an ongoing basis. "The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles," Mayes told a press conference in Chicago. Mayes declined to identify the other companies her office was investigating. She said her office had been in contact with Arizona banks, but declined to name them or give their responses. A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The banking industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. Reuters reported last month that major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions. Mayes' comments come two days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI for allegedly developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had carried out cyberattacks independently. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on that lawsuit, but the company has â acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.” (Reporting by David Thomas; Editing by Peter Henderson and Kate Mayberry) Sorry, there are no recent results for popular images. Michigan docs wary with loss of country's measles elimination status
articles.description: Doctors face a challenge in identifying measles infections as the virus spread.
articles.content: The Centers for Disease Control is urging doctors — many of whom may not have encountered a measles case in their practice — to be on the lookout for signs of the disease, now that the U.S. has lost its 26-year measles elimination status.( Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)State health officials are now monitoring 31 confirmed cases of measles in Michigan. The latest outbreaks are centered in St. Joseph and Hillsdale counties, where 12 people have come down with disease, according to the Branch-Hillsdale-St. Joseph Community Health Agency. Six are in Hillsdale county and six are in Saint Joseph County.Medical professionals are bracing for more, now that the United States has lost its measles-elimination status. The designation means that active cases are present in numbers suggesting the disease has been transmitted for 12 months or more, uninterrupted.Measles is a viral disease that has been less common in the United States over the past 20 years. It’s highly contagious, and can survive airborne up to two hours. In recent years, a combination of vaccine hesitation, public confusion and changes of federal policy have led an increasing number of parents to skip their children’s MMR vaccinations.Dr. Peter Gulick is a professor of osteopathic medicine at Michigan State University who specializes in infectious diseases. He shared concerns about preparedness among primary care providers across the state.“It's been a disease that you talk about as more of a history-type of thing … since there's been total control since 2000 and we haven't had any cases until recently,” Gulick said.Gulick participates in Project ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes), an outreach from MSU’s College of Osteopathic Medicine to providers in rural areas of the state to strengthen preventive care and share information. He’s planning to repeat a session he led a few months ago on best practices for spotting, isolating, and treating measles infection.The dangers to measles patients often rest with the risk of complications like encephalitis or pneumonia — but Gulick added an even more serious possibility for patients is the way measles compromises the body’s immune system, opening the door to any number of lethal problems, especially among the very young.“It can be a long lasting problem where it can make you very susceptible to infections for a long period of time.”Health departments are encouraging people to check their measles vaccination status, and to get the vaccine if they haven’t.Doctors have recommended a two-dose vaccination that covers measles, as well as mumps and rubella, for children starting at 12 to 15 months old, with a second dose for kids age 4-6.The vast majority of people who are vaccinated experience lifetime protection from the disease.

articles.title: Lawsuit challenges SNAP restrictions on sugary drinks, food in 18 states
articles.description: A lawsuit filed Wednesday seeks to block more states from restricting what kind of items food stamp recipients can buy. Led by the National Center for Law and Economic Justice, the class action lawsuit seeks to strike down restrictions on products such as candy and soda in 18 states for recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition […]
articles.content: Sodas and chips are displayed at a convenience store in New York City. A new lawsuit targets restrictions on sugary drinks and foods for food stamp recipients across 18 states. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)A lawsuit filed Wednesday seeks to block more states from restricting what kind of items food stamp recipients can buy. Led by the National Center for Law and Economic Justice, the class action lawsuit seeks to strike down restrictions on products such as candy and soda in 18 states for recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. It targets Arkansas, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Virginia and Wyoming. In previous litigation, a judge already blocked state and federal efforts to use waivers to restrict SNAP purchases in Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia. “These unlawful waivers serve as a backdoor method to restrict access to SNAP,” Katharine Deabler-Meadows, senior attorney at the national center, said in a Wednesday news release. “Our lawsuit seeks to hold the Trump administration accountable for violating the law and causing unprecedented chaos for SNAP recipients and retailers alike.” The Trump administration has encouraged states to seek federal waivers restricting what kinds of purchases can be made with SNAP, which has traditionally allowed recipients broad autonomy to select their own groceries. Those waivers have targeted a variety of products but generally focus on sugary beverages and candies. Hawaii’s waiver restricts only the purchases of soft drinks, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. But Florida’s waiver restricts purchases of soda, energy drinks, candy and prepared desserts. The federal government argues those restrictions divert taxpayer dollars away from food purchases that fuel the nation’s epidemics of diabetes and other chronic diseases. “These waivers help put real food back at the center of the program and empower states to lead the charge in protecting public health,” U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement last year. Critics say the changes could harm people in food deserts, where healthy options are limited, and take away recipients’ power to make their own food choices. In the lawsuit, plaintiffs argue that the changes have harmed their health. One Idaho plaintiff said she had multiple chronic health conditions including autoimmune conditions that make it difficult for her to regulate her blood pressure, heart rate and blood sugar levels. She relies on electrolyte-infused drinks and easy-to-eat foods, such as nutrition and granola bars that are now restricted in Idaho. “Since the waiver was implemented, she has frequently been dehydrated, and her kidney function, digestion, and autonomic function, which affect her heart and ability to remain upright, have worsened,” the lawsuit said. Another plaintiff in Oklahoma said she relied on easy-to-prepare foods as she lives in an extended-stay hotel without a kitchen. With upper gastrointestinal issues that cause discomfort, she drinks soda to relieve gas that gets trapped in her esophagus. But those beverages are now restricted under Oklahoma’s waiver. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia, argues that USDA lacks the legal authority to use waivers to undertake such large-scale change to SNAP’s structure. USDA said the department does not comment on pending litigation. Editor’s note: This story was updated to include USDA’s response. If you or a loved one needs help during a mental health crisis, call or text 988, or visit 988helpline.org. Help is available for veterans and nonveterans alike. WASHINGTON — Federal regulators could be on the cusp of approving psychedelic-assisted mental health treatment for veterans, but lawmakers asked tough questions Wednesday of Trump administration officials over whether the Department of Veterans Affairs can meet patients’ needs, and if federal law enforcement and health agencies are on the same page. Just over 2 million veterans suffer with treatment-resistant depression, and approximately 180,000 of them would likely meet the criteria for treatment with psychedelic compounds, including MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, DMT and ibogaine, according to the Veterans Health Administration. Members of the House Committee on Veterans Affairs Subcommittee on Health grilled officials for roughly two and a half hours during an afternoon hearing contemplating how the VA should implement the labor-intensive treatments if given the green light by the Food and Drug Administration. Nearly 6,500 veterans died by suicide in 2024, according to the latest Veterans Affairs Suicide Prevention Annual Report, published in September. “Something needs to change,” said subcommittee chair Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who said despite prevention efforts, the numbers have remained “stubbornly stagnant.” “When I came to Congress in 2021, I didn’t think I’d be sitting here today advocating for these emerging breakthrough therapies, but in meeting with veterans from all walks of life, I have found the effectiveness of these treatments and am willing to advance it as potential hope,” said Miller-Meeks, who recently lost her bid for reelection. Miller-Meeks, an Army veteran and ophthalmologist, cited randomized clinical trials for MDMA-assisted therapies that commenced this year at VA facilities in Rhode Island and Connecticut, both of which resulted from funding allocated in 2024. Miller-Meeks also praised President Donald Trump’s April executive order directing the FDA to work with other agencies, including the VA, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Department of Health and Human Services to remove barriers, like drug enforcement classification, that complicate testing the treatments. The possibility of new treatments was met with optimism on both sides of the aisle. The subcommittee’s ranking member Rep. Julia Brownley, D-Calif., said the clinical trials are “extremely welcome news and will change lives for the better.” “At the same time, we must not lose sight of the fact that this treatment, much like the ones already in use today, will not be a panacea for everyone,” she said. “Even as VA works to build its capacity to provide access to these drugs, we must continue to maintain and strengthen the continuum of mental healthcare at VA.” Staff reductions present problem During questioning Brownley expressed concern about VA’s ability to implement the new treatments in the wake of staff reductions under the Trump administration, if the FDA moves forward. “Will VA be hiring additional workforce to meet the expected demand for these treatments and ensure existing workforce is not overtaxed if these treatments are approved in the next several months?” Brownley asked. Andrew Gradison, a Veterans Health Administration senior adviser who testified, acknowledged the treatments are “extremely labor intensive” and that along with preparation protocols, “dosing sessions alone can last six to eight hours.” “We’ve conducted extensive analysis of the amount of staff time that goes into these treatments,” Gradison said. “We want to make sure that all of our initial implementation sites have the resources they need, not to have a detrimental impact on mental health access at large.” Gradison told the panel that VA has identified 10 initial sites where treatment could occur, but would not publicly divulge every location. He said he would provide a list to all committee members within 30 days. Rep. Herb Conaway, D-N.J., said “most of them are on the coast.” “I see a lot in California. I see New Haven, Connecticut. I don’t see any in the Southeast. New York is on this list as well. Do you believe that you have, even with those that you’ve established as possibly being ready, that you’re sufficiently covering the country?” Conaway, a medical doctor, asked. Dr. Ilse Wiechers, deputy assistant under secretary for health for patient care services with VA’s Veterans Health Administration, told Conaway, “The reason you see the selected sites that you do is because those are the sites that we have evaluated to be the most likely to be successful in implementing this early on. “We are going to use that experience from those experienced sites,” she added. Working with DEA All the drugs under review remain categorized as Schedule I substances by federal law enforcement. Michigan Republican Rep. Jack Bergman, a retired U.S. Marine Corps lieutenant general, asked the expert panel, “What should VA be working out with DEA now, and where do you expect control substance requirements to cause the most delay?” Marion Coe, director of clinical development and postmarketing surveillance at the healthcare industry consulting firm Pinney Associates, Inc., said the research involving these chemical compounds, particularly being able to legally store them, is a “complicated process.” “VA and DEA ideally would work together to reduce these bureaucratic hurdles to make research easier,” she said. “This will all be made simpler after approval and rescheduling of these drugs.”

(Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)WASHINGTON — Vermont independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he intends to focus on universal healthcare and oversight investigations when he takes over as chairman of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year. Sanders, who has served as ranking member on the panel during this session of Congress, said on a call with reporters that he also intends to take a “hard look at the impact of AI and robotics on the well-being of the American people.” The country’s current healthcare system, he said, “is broken, it is dysfunctional and it is extraordinarily cruel.” Sanders said he wants to move the country toward universal healthcare, which he said “should be a ‘Medicare for All,’ single payer program.” “It’s not a radical idea, it’s not a fringe idea,” he said, referring to a KFF poll conducted in mid-September that showed 66% of respondents support a national health plan when told it would “guarantee health insurance for all Americans.” The level of support was about the same, 75%, when people were told it would “eliminate all insurance premiums and reduce out-of-pocket costs for most Americans.” A slight majority, 52%, of respondents said they’d support a Medicare for All-type plan when told it would “eliminate private health insurance companies.” Approval dropped to 38% when those polled were told it could “threaten the current Medicare program” and then to 35% when informed it would “require most Americans to pay more in taxes.” Sanders said on the call he appreciated that House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker next Congress, has said he supports a transition of sorts that would lower the age of eligibility for Medicare from 65 to 55; ensure it covers children; and expand coverage to dental, hearing and vision. “I think the word is getting out that it is no longer, from a political point of view, from a policy point of view, good enough to tinker around the edges,” Sanders said. Investigating RFK Jr.’s management of HHS When it comes to investigations, he said, the committee will likely take a look at how Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has managed the department, including the ongoing measles outbreak. “That is certainly one area that needs investigation,” Sanders said. “There are many more.” The HELP Committee will look into how health insurance companies are “ripping off the American people” and why pharmaceutical companies charge higher prices for certain drugs than they do in other countries. While many of the policy goals and investigations Sanders plans to pursue are unlikely to get support from Republicans, he said there are some areas of overlap that could lead to bipartisanship. When asked about the Make America Healthy Again movement that has been center stage during the Trump administration, Sanders told reporters it’s unlikely he ever agrees with members of the movement on vaccines, but that there could be common ground on health foods and better access to healthcare. “To the degree that we can work with the MAHA people, we want to see labeling, good labeling on food packages that we don’t have right now,” he said. “I would like to see junk food advertising off of the TV airwaves. So I think there are some areas that we can work with. Obviously there are some other areas where we have profound disagreements.” Sanders said there may be some areas of overlap with Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, who will likely become the top Republican on the committee next year. “Rand, needless to say philosophically, holds a slightly different point of view than I do,” he said. But Sanders added that Paul has shown “courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year” and that the two have worked together on civil liberties and privacy issues.

articles.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit
articles.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit, rather than reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. The short answer is AI, but not in the way you might expect.
articles.content: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying he’s replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He’s saying he’s reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI. The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit. “Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he explained. For some people, “that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?” he added, “but, I mean, it has to be done.” He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product.” He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs.” But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn’t grow up as an AI-first company. “So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?” he said. “It’s going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, ‘Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.’” When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, “We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don’t have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution.” He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. “All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity.” In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. articles.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani sat down with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the 2026 DealBook Summit at Lincoln Center for a wide-ranging conversation on the midterms, his working relationship with President Trump, taxing the rich, antisemitism, housing, and the city’s plan for public supermarkets. The 35-year-old Democratic Socialist mayor laid out his vision for making New York City more affordable while defending his approach to business leaders, billionaires and Wall Street. Here is the full transcript below: ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:00:01 – 00:01:10): The mayor is here. He ran for office, as you know, vowing to make the city of 8.5 million people more affordable. He is 35 years old, Democratic Socialist, and we’re going to talk this afternoon about everything. We’re going to talk about the midterms, taxes, capitalism, socialism, AI, billionaires, and the greatest city in the world. Mr. Mayor, thank you for being here. I want to get your reaction to the midterms, but I really want to actually ask you this as it relates to the Democratic Party today. So Treasury Secretary Bessent, who was sitting where you were a year ago, told us that you are not the fringe Democratic left anymore. It’s the mainstream of the Democratic And I’m curious whether you think that that is true, and that whether this midterm was really a repudiation of the current administration or was an affirmative vote for your brand of democratic socialism. ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:01:11 – 00:02:06): Well, first I have to say, comrades, it’s great to be here at the largest DSA meeting Lincoln Center has ever seen. And it’s a real pleasure to be here with you as well, Andrew. I think that the midterms were a reflection of working-class Americans’ hunger for a new kind of politics, and a politics that can deliver change that they can feel in their wallets. And what you see, whether you’re looking at candidates, no matter how they describe themselves, is a specificity of purpose. In James Talarico, you see a call for universal pre-K. Keisha Lance Bottoms, you are seeing the importance of streamlining affordable housing production. If you’re looking at Michigan’s governor’s race, you’re seeing a data moratorium. These are the kinds of things that have motivated many to not just repudiate federal policies that have made their lives more expensive, but also to call for a different kind of approach in what politics can actually deliver to working people’s lives. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:02:06 – 00:02:15): So the president says he wants to work with Democrats, said it on 60 Minutes. A, do you believe him? And B, if so, what does that look like? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:02:16 – 00:02:40): Well, I can tell you from my personal experience that as someone who has significant policy disagreements with the president, that I have worked with the president over the course of the time that I’ve been the mayor of our city. And I’ll give you an example of what it looks like. The federal government had announced that they were going to change the stocking requirements for small businesses to be SNAP authorized. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:02:40 – 00:02:41): Just happened, yes. ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:02:41 – 00:03:39): And these were requirements that put small businesses across the country and bodegas here in New York City into a state of panic. Because if they weren’t able to comply, the federal government was threatening to strip them of their SNAP status. And in places like the Bronx, SNAP contributes up to 30% of revenue for an individual bodega. And so, yes, I wrote a letter to the secretary. About how this is an issue that businesses here in New York City are facing, businesses across the country are facing. And to your question, I then picked up the phone and called the president to make the case on behalf of New York City. And I made the case that when it comes to these kinds of requirements, the panic that it’s putting small businesses under and the impact that would have on New Yorkers’ lives as well, who rely on that small business for the food that they’re purchasing, this was something that needed to be extended.And the president made the decision to extend it by at least 3 months. And in doing that, providing relief for businesses across the entire country. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:03:39 – 00:04:32): Can you explain the bromance? No, I— because I think we all watch it both with fascination and some level of bafflement, given some of the things that he said about you, calling you a communist before you were elected, and some of the things that you’ve said about him, Namely that you called him a fascist. And so I want to understand how the phone call works, but I’m also curious, and I think this actually speaks to maybe how Democrats and Republicans in this case work together. I have noticed, and you can correct me if I’m wrong, you don’t actually criticize him that often in public. You did during the election, but I would say in this particular role. On ICE, yes, you have. But for the most part, I think you watch your words. And I wanted to understand that on just a very personal level. ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:04:33 – 00:05:48): Well, I’ll go through your first question, then I’ll come to this one. I think on the practical level of how does this work, I just told you about bodegas, and most people in this room know exactly what a bodega is. Usually when you’re calling someone at a national level, they might not be as familiar with the intricacies of New York City. The president is very familiar. I do not have to explain what a bodega is to the president. And in fact, the first time I met the president, this is in the Oval Office, maybe in, I think it was about November, soon after I’d won the election. We sat down in the Oval Office and discussed zoning in Midtown Manhattan. We discussed community boards. We discussed the process by which any of these large-scale developments can get built. And to me, that’s a reflection of the fact that For all that he’s the President of the United States, he’s also the most famous developer the city has ever seen. And I’m also not shy about the places in which we have serious disagreement, because I think that it is incumbent upon us in elected office to be honest about those places of disagreement and also have these conversations so long as they can deliver for the people of the city. And so you’ve said it, it’s on ICE, it’s also on the Iran war, it’s also on an immense amount of domestic policy, and making that clear both in private and also in public. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:05:49 – 00:05:51): Would you still call him a fascist? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:05:51 – 00:05:51): Yes. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:05:52 – 00:05:58): You would? Has he ever asked you about that? Have you ever said, “What’s this? How is this going to work?” ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:05:59 – 00:06:08): I’ll keep the conversations between the president and myself private, but I will tell you that we both know how we feel about the other’s policies, and we both love the same city. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:06:08 – 00:06:16): But let me ask you in this context, ’cause I was watching, And I know you guys might have seen this too. President Trump came to visit you, Gracie Mansion. ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:06:16 – 00:06:16): Yes. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:06:16 – 00:07:08): And this is when he was trying to actually push out a number of media organizations at the White House. And you had the media organizations there at Gracie Mansion. And he, of course, goes on a sort of a thing about the “fake news” and all of that. And you don’t really say they’re not fake news or this or that. You sort of, through demonstration by having them there, that’s what it is. But you don’t go on a sort of a defense of the media industry, which, by the way, your constituents here in New York is the— and I know, and I was curious about that because I’m watching this happen and I’m seeing him criticize the media. And I think that you have— you may not love the media stories all the time, but I think you have a very different view of this. But I thought to myself, you know what, maybe he’s holding his tongue. And so how do you feel about the tongue, holding the tongue? And do you think you have to? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:07:09 – 00:07:12): I think so long as the tongue tells the truth, then you’re being— ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:07:12 – 00:07:17): But does it? That’s the question. Do you ever feel like you’re pretending because you have to sort of make it work? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:07:18 – 00:08:06): No, I feel like I am being honest to myself. I’m being honest to the city. And I think also choosing when meeting with the president, when speaking to the president, to focus on any possible area of commonality. And the reason for that is the stakes are so immense. The second time I met the president at the White House, I left the White House having secured an agreement to release a New Yorker who was detained by ICE that morning. Later on, we had a phone call where I was able to secure a visa for a mother who would otherwise have had to grieve her son from thousands of miles away. With this agreement for small businesses across the country, there are quite literally small businesses that will be able to stay open as a result of it. And so to me, it comes back to there is a responsibility to deliver. And that is also why you have to speak to anyone that could help you to deliver. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:08:07 – 00:08:35): You’re the mayor of New York, but there have been a whole number of reports that have suggested that you may want to play a larger role in the country, in future elections. What is your ambition beyond being the mayor itself? Because there were some meetings with union leaders about sort of how to get other people in the Democratic Party around the country elected. The question is, how— what kind of role are you planning to play in all of this? How should we see you? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:08:35 – 00:08:46): Well, I think I’m proud to be the first mayor of New York City in a long time who is not going to run for president. And I think it’s important to say that to people of New York City. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:08:46 – 00:08:47): Would you if you could? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:08:48 – 00:09:33): No. I’m very— this is the best job in the world. You get to wake up and go to sleep in New York City every single day. And yes, we all love New York. I think in terms of the role, it’s a recognition of the fact that what we want to see in our politics, whether it’s in Astoria or Allentown or Albuquerque, is an approach that puts the struggles of working-class people at the center. Because what we have forgotten in our politics across the entire nation is that there is only one majority in this country, and that’s the working class. And yet, when you look at the policies that have been put forward, it’s as if that’s been completely forgotten. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:09:34 – 00:09:50): Back in March, you signed a petition calling AOC the most viable left contender for president. Have you spoken to her, and what do you think the chances are that that she runs for president? Would you prefer that she runs for Senate? What do you want out of all this? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:09:51 – 00:10:00): Yes, I have spoken with the congresswoman. We are in regular touch. And what I would say is that whatever she chooses to do, she will do it incredibly. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:10:00 – 00:10:01): What do you think she’ll do? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:10:02 – 00:10:02): I don’t know. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:10:02 – 00:10:04): What’s your best guess today? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:10:04 – 00:10:11): You had the Polymarket guy right before me. He’s got agents in the back trading right now on whether or not she does it. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:10:12 – 00:10:14): Have you ever traded, by the way, on a Kalshi or a Polymarket? ZOHRAN MAMDANI (00:10:15 – 00:10:15): No, I have not. ANDREW ROSS SORKIN (00:10:15 – 00:10:16): You have not? Okay. ZOHRAN MAMDANI

articles.content: Zohran Mamdani is defending his relationship with President Donald Trump. The New York City mayor, 34, was on hand at the New York Times DealBook Summit — the annual business, policy and culture conference hosted by the Times and led by columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin — where he opened up about what Sorkin, 49, called his “bromance” with the 80-year-old president. “On the practical level of how does this work, I just told you about bodegas, and most people in this room know exactly what a bodega is. Usually, when you’re calling someone at a national level, they might not be as familiar with the intricacies of New York City,” Mamdani said of Trump, per a clip shared from the summit on X. “The president is very familiar. I do not have to explain what a bodega is to the president.” “I’m also not shy about the places in which we have serious disagreement,” he continued in another clip shared from the summit, before sharing his advice for incoming Democrats following the midterm election’s big, blue wave. “Because I think that it is incumbent upon us in elected office to be honest about those places of disagreement, and also have these conversations so long as they can deliver for the people of the city. It’s on ICE, it’s also on the Iran war, it’s also an immense amount of domestic policy, and making that clear in private, but also in public.” While they’ve managed to work together over some of the issues that plague New Yorkers, when asked by Sorkin if he still thinks Trump is a fascist, Mamdani doubled down, simply replying, “Yes.” As for whether Trump has questioned the mayor on his views of him as the leader of the free world, Mamdani responded in a slightly cagier way, telling Sorkin, “I’ll keep conversations between the president and myself private, but I will tell you, we both know how we feel about the other’s policies, and we both love the same city.” The politicians have indeed disagreed on plenty, particularly in Mamdani’s lead-up to becoming New York City’s first Muslim mayor, with the president labeling the Democratic Socialist a “communist lunatic.” The Apprentice alum has since dialed back those insults following the pair’s 2025 meeting at the White House, where Trump famously complimented his looks and said he’d feel comfortable living in New York City under Mamdani’s leadership. The pair even worked together as recently as this month, with Mamdani teaming up with Trump to secure a 90-day delay for the city’s beloved bodegas to comply with new federal food-stamp rules, the New York Post reports, giving bodegas more time to meet the new guidelines — which require SNAP-authorized retailers, including the city’s small shops — to stock seven varieties each of dairy, grains, proteins and produce as opposed to the current three. articles.title: Ukraine blew up Putin’s bridge using relay drones to bypass Starlink limits
articles.description: Ukraine's strike used homegrown tech while adapting battlefield lessons from its adversary.
articles.content: A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in. On the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War update. Russian sources claimed several hundred Ukrainian drones first overwhelmed Russian air defenses to pave the way for remote-controlled missile strikes focused on the bridge, with the latter prominently including Ukraine’s homegrown Flamingo cruise missile. The Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times. Each networked drone acts as a relay node to extend the communication link between human operators and remotely piloted missiles and strike drones. Russia began using the technique to support long-range drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian cities.Read full article Comments

articles.content: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella predicts that the rise of AI agents is going to reshape the economics of the internet, impacting the business models of the companies that rely on advertising and what he referred to as “human web” traffic. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the tech executive argued that the shift to an agentic web could change which companies pay others for traffic and for transactions, similar to how the transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google did years ago. “The current aggregators who have a business model which was for the human web will get, in some sense, reshuffled,” said Nadella. “And if you were monetizing ads because of the eyeballs, you now have to probably get down to essentially maybe CPC [cost-per-click] wins; maybe it’s more transactional,” he continued. “And so if you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will.” The discussion turned to Amazon and its decision to block AI agents from accessing its retail website, preventing them from browsing its catalog and making purchases on behalf of their users. Nadella suggested that companies trying to protect their existing business models could lose out to others that are more willing to embrace the AI agents. For instance, if Amazon continues blocking agents, another shopping platform such as Shopify, could allow them, and gain an advantage. “I think this is going to be interesting,” he said, speaking to the changing models. “It’s the same thing that’s happening in other categories, right? Which is, if you’re in love with a particular business model, you have to kind of scramble,” he said. articles.title: Whitmer reflects on two terms as governor while hosting her final turkey pardon
articles.description: With the end of her 8-year tenure as governor soon to come to a close, Gretchen Whitmer stood outside the Capitol on Wednesday to fulfill a key ceremonial duty for the last time. Gathering with Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development Director Tim Boring, members of the Durand Future Farmers of America and the […]
articles.content: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer held her final turkey pardon on Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)With the end of her 8-year tenure as governor soon to come to a close, Gretchen Whitmer stood outside the Capitol on Wednesday to fulfill a key ceremonial duty for the last time. Gathering with Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development Director Tim Boring, members of the Durand Future Farmers of America and the heads of the Ann Arbor-based Creature Conservancy, Whitmer issued her final turkey pardon, delivering this year’s bird, Sparty, from a future on the Thanksgiving table Named after the Michigan State University mascot, Sparty is the sixth Turkey Whitmer has pardoned since she began the tradition in 2022, granting clemency to Mitch. E. Gander. Over the past four years she’s also exonerated Dolly Pardon, Aidan Cluckinson and, most recently, Vernors and Faygo. “Out of all the traditions I have been a part of, this is one of the ones that I will miss the most,” Whitmer said. She likened her role of governor to preparing Thanksgiving dinner for the entire extended family. “You gotta make sure there’s enough seats at the table for everyone, you cater solutions to every dietary restriction and need, and still people are a little underwhelmed at times, and every year you deliver a balanced, bipartisan, basted butterball of a budget, right?” Whitmer said. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pardoned Sparty, a Norfolk black heritage turkey, at her final turkey pardon on Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance) Reflecting on her almost eight years in office, the governor pointed to several of her crowning achievements on kitchen table issues, including expanding access to free Pre-K and community college, repealing the retirement tax, expanding the working families tax credit and providing free breakfast and lunch for Michigan students. As for Sparty? She’ll live the rest of her life as an animal ambassador at The Creature Conservancy, where founder and Head Curator Steve Marsh says they’ve recently started a program called “barnyard buddies” to promote rural animals and agriculture. However, Whitmer’s time as governor is not done yet, and lawmakers in the Michigan House and Senate are still scheduled to meet in the coming weeks. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer takes question from reporters following her final turkey pardon, Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance) While taking questions from reporters after the turkey pardon, Whitmer pointed to housing as one area where her office and members of the Democratic-led Senate and the Republican-led House could make some progress before the year is done. Earlier this year, Republicans and Democrats in the House came together to put forth legislation aimed at updating the state’s zoning laws to cut down on unnecessary costs and delays in building new housing. However the policies have yet to receive a vote in the House Government Operations Committee following a hearing earlier this year. “There are a lot of pieces of it that I think we could find common ground and get done,” Whitmer said. While there are other items on the governor’s agenda, Whitmer said it will ultimately depend on what the appetite is from lawmakers and how much work they want to get done.

articles.title: UK's Prince Harry sees 'big separation' between US administration, public on support for Ukraine
articles.description: UK's Prince Harry sees 'big separation' between US administration, public on support for Ukraine AP News Prince Harry says he’d return to the military to face Russia if needed CNN Prince Harry, after Ukraine trip, warns on threat from Russia BBC Prince Harry interview in full: Those of us who have served should be ready to serve again The Telegraph Prince Harry: I’ll rejoin the army if the need is there The Times
articles.content: LONDON (AP) — Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump Administration’s stance and that of the American people. Harry, a British Army veteran who returned to his home country last summer after six years in California, also said he believes Britain has been in conflict with Russia for the past decade and that he is ready to serve in the military once again if he is called upon to do so. The comments came in an interview with The Daily Telegraph that took place last weekend during Harry’s fourth visit to Ukraine since the full-scale Russian invasion. The newspaper published a story about the interview on Wednesday and is scheduled to release the full interview in a podcast that will be posted at midnight London time (0000 GMT). “I think there’s been a big separation between what American society feel regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in this case an administration, that was perhaps thinking about it differently,” Harry said. Harry traveled to Ukraine last weekend to meet with athletes who are preparing to take part in the 2027 Invictus Games, the Paralympic-style competition he founded to inspire wounded veterans. Next year’s games will take place in Birmingham, England. The prince is not a working member of the royal family and traveled to Ukraine as a private citizen. Harry said now is the time for Britain and its allies to double their support for Ukraine to ensure that it defeats Russia at a time when Moscow is trying to stir up divisions within European society. British intelligence and military officials are increasingly warning about sabotage, disinformation campaigns and other so-called hybrid attacks carried out by Russian operatives to destabilize western societies. “I think the threat has been there and been consistently there for the last 15 years,” Harry said. “Just because there’s not drones, bullets and rockets flying at us, that doesn’t mean that we’re not at war. I feel like we’ve been at war for the last decade.” Harry, who was deployed to Afghanistan twice during his military career, said veterans should be ready to serve again. “If the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel,” he said.

articles.content: In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump's pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation. Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy's decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats. In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA's current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn't say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is "quite lethal" or that children are given vaccine doses the "size of a soda bottle." articles.title: How caregivers can modify holiday plans to accommodate older adults
articles.description: Planning ahead, setting limitations, and asking for help during the holidays while caregiving may provide some relief during gatherings. The post How caregivers can modify holiday plans to accommodate older adults appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: Planning ahead, setting limitations, and asking for help during the holidays while caregiving may provide some relief during gatherings. More than 63 million Americans are in-family caregivers. Advocates say they often feel overwhelmed, isolated and unable to take care of themselves. Amanda Leggett is an associate professor at the Wayne State Institute of Gerontology and the Department of Psychology. She studies caregiving styles, with a focus on family care for individuals with dementia. She says there are five caregiving styles: the externalizer, individualist, learner, adapter and nurturer. The caregiving styles range in adaptive strategies for caring for individuals. “We realize not all caregivers are alike, right? We’re all individuals, just like everyone has kind of a unique personality, individuals have unique approaches to care,” she says. During National Family Caregivers Month, Leggett says caregiving may come up during the holiday season. She suggests speaking with family members about changing expectations, limitations, and help as needed to cater to individuals who require caregiving. “I want to tell family caregivers: we need to relax some of those expectations of what we think the holidays are going to look like,” she says. Leggett notes that maintaining routines, taking breaks or keeping gatherings short may work better for caregivers caring for people with dementia. “As much as we can kind of cater the holiday celebrations around that routine…a chance for people to take a break amidst the holiday chaos might be really helpful,” she explains. Leggett adds that caregivers can give family members a heads-up about changes they may see alongside suggestions on how other family members, friends or neighbors can step up. “If you’re another friend or family, don’t wait to be asked,” she says. Leggett acknowledges the grief that pops up during the holidays, too. She states that caregivers and their relatives are justified in reminiscing about what used to be. She also challenges them to think about what has changed and how can it be properly managed. “It’s 100% okay to feel those emotions and sit with them, but also, look for the moments of joy.” People can also honor loved ones who are no longer here during the holidays, too. “Maybe it’s looking through old photographs or sharing family videos…looking back on some of those prior holiday memories… to reflect on them,” Leggett says. She shares that there is a place for new familial experiences that carry the joy of the past in the new traditions they create. “There’s ways to kind of look back on the memories and the joy of these prior holidays together, but also think about new things that you might establish as a family that will also bring some joy and excitement in moving forward,” she shares. Leggett says it’s also okay for caregivers to seek short-term caregiving assistance through asking others outside of the family to help out during the holidays. “Caregivers often really struggle with the willingness to accept help or to ask for help. It’s okay to do that,” she says. “I always say to my caregivers, ‘we can’t pour from an empty cup.'”

Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security
articles.description: Hardened defaults align with DoD standards, but there may be growing pains.
articles.content: Microsoft's Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core. Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency's (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG). STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: "The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened." The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance.Read full article Comments
