Environmental Justice Advocates Urge NYC to Adopt Mayor Mamdani’s First Climate and Environmental Justice Regulation
articles.content: WISER will clean up warehouse and diesel pollution to give NYC clean air and safer streets; Air pollution from operations disproportionally impacts communities of color who experience high exposure to diesel truck pollution This Tuesday, the NYC Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) officially launched the rulemaking process for Mayor Zohran Mamdani administration’s first climate and environmental justice regulation, Warehouse Indirect Source Emissions Reduction (WISER) program. Environmental justice and community advocates urge New York City to swiftly adopt a strong WISER rule, a major public health and environmental justice policy that holds large warehouse operators accountable for pollution, traffic, and health impacts from mega-warehouse delivery facilities. Diesel pollution from warehouse-related truck traffic is linked to asthma, heart disease, cognitive impairment, and premature death. Research by the Environmental Defense Fund estimates that diesel pollution contributes to more than 10,000 new childhood asthma cases in New York City each year. These impacts fall disproportionately on environmental justice communities, which contain a majority of warehouse facilities despite representing a small share of the state’s geography. Recent analysis highlights the growing harms of e-commerce delivery operations on New York City’s streets and neighborhoods. In just four years, Amazon delivery vehicles were ticketed thousands of times for blocking bus lanes, speeding in school zones, and obstructing bike lanes and crosswalks. In neighborhoods where last-mile facilities have opened, truck-related crashes have increased by 146%. At the same time, 90% of New York City’s goods movement relies on trucks, far exceeding the national average. During Tuesday’s NYC Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) public meeting on the WISER draft Scope of Work, advocates emphasized that the City must act swiftly to drive a robust program and ensure the final rule delivers meaningful pollution reductions. The rule is built on a model of proven success. Southern California air regulators adopted a similar rule and warehouses have complied while continuing to grow. The southern California warehouse rule has brought significant benefits for communities over-burdened by air pollution, reducing harmful NOx pollution by around 1.5 tons per day. The rule raised over $60 million in revenue to improve community air quality, despite mitigation fees only accounting for 5% of total compliance. “We welcome the launch of the Warehouse Indirect Source Emissions Reduction (WISER) program, the first climate and environmental justice regulation by the Mamdani administration. We urge New York City leadership to move quickly to adopt a strong final rule. Communities living near last-mile warehouses have borne the brunt of diesel truck pollution for far too long. DEP must ensure the rule drives real emissions reductions and limits combustion-based vehicles for clean air and safe New York City streets.” The Last-Mile Coalition, a citywide coalition of environmental justice and public health advocates fighting to regulate last-mile trucking facilities in New York City. Earthjustice is the premier nonprofit environmental law organization. We wield the power of law and the strength of partnership to protect people's health, to preserve magnificent places and wildlife, to advance clean energy, and to combat climate change. We are here because the earth needs a good lawyer. “Attacks against the National Environmental Policy Act are cowardly attempts to silence all of us, including the very people who build the infrastructure that makes this country prosper.”

articles.title: Advocates, state representative criticize ‘bad faith’ appointment to sentencing commission
articles.description: State Rep. Kara Hope (D-Holt) joined criminal justice advocates Wednesday to criticize the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission, which was established in 2024 to examine the state’s sentencing laws and procedures. Jones was appointed not because of his previous legislative experience or his time as Eaton County Sheriff […]
articles.content: State Rep. Kara Hope (D-Holt) speaks at a press conference criticizing the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission in a seat reserved for formerly incarcerated individuals. Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)State Rep. Kara Hope (D-Holt) joined criminal justice advocates Wednesday to criticize the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission, which was established in 2024 to examine the state’s sentencing laws and procedures. Jones was appointed not because of his previous legislative experience or his time as Eaton County Sheriff — but instead to fill a seat designed for a previously incarcerated person, based on a single night spent in jail after being arrested for drunk driving in February. “Power can sometimes be misused, and I think that’s what we saw here,” Hope said. “Misused to shut out the very people that we met to give a seat at the table, and that’s why I’m here. That’s why we’re all here, to demand that it never happens again.” Jones was appointed to the commission, which held its first meeting in May, by outgoing Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt (R-Porter Township). Ken Nixon, director of outreach and community partnerships for Safe and Just Michigan, likened the appointment to filling a seat intended for a judge with “someone who once sat in a courtroom.” “When the Legislature built this commission, it made a choice. It said judges get a voice, prosecutors get a voice, law enforcement gets a voice, and people who have actually lived under these sentences get a voice too,” Nixon said. “That seat was a promise, and right now that promise isn’t being kept. One night in the county jail is a bad weekend. Five years in prison changes your life. It changes your family. It changes whether your kids know you. It changes whether you can find a job or a place to live when you come home. Those are consequences this commission is supposed to weigh, and the people who carry them are the experts nobody has been asking.” Ken Nixon, the director of outreach and community partnerships for Safe and Just Michigan, speaks at a press conference criticizing the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission in a seat reserved for formerly incarcerated individuals. Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)José Burgos, a policy advocate for the Campaign for the Fair Sentencing of Youth, speaks at a press conference criticizing the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission in a seat reserved for formerly incarcerated individuals. Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Edward Sanders, the founder and CEO of Alternative Sentencing and Reentry Solutions, speaks at a press conference criticizing the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission in a seat reserved for formerly incarcerated individuals. Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance) A request for comment was made to both Jones and the commission. This story will be updated when a response is received. Edward Sanders, the founder and CEO of Alternative Sentencing and Reentry Solutions, who was incarcerated in a Michigan prison for over 40 years, similarly said that a person with Jones’ experience could not personally speak to the impacts on education, employment, or emotional and physical development of someone who has spent significant time in custody — especially someone who was first incarcerated as a minor, as Sanders was. “It’s more likely that that child would die a premature death. It’s more likely that that child’s employment outcome would look different after that experience. It’s more likely that that child’s mental state would deteriorate,” he said. “A person that has spent a day in jail cannot share that with you. Not one day could that person take and explain to you what that meant or will mean for that child.” Hope emphasized throughout the press conference that her problem is not with Jones specifically, but instead with the fact that he was appointed in what she called bad faith to a seat intended for someone with significant experience in Michigan’s carceral system. “This isn’t about him personally,” she said. “It’s about reading the statute in bad faith and doing something that’s completely contrary to the intent of the drafters and all the advocates who worked so hard on this.” Nixon, who was previously incarcerated himself, also emphasized that his criticisms were not about Jones as an individual, but that it was “heartbreaking” to have a member on the commission in that seat who “can’t speak to any of the things that we’ve been through or we’ve seen or the struggles of reentry, the struggles of trying to fight your way back into society after that.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Hope introduced a bill in the state House on Nov. 5 to alter the language that dictates the commission’s membership. The law, as currently written, states that the commission’s membership will include “One individual who was previously incarcerated,” and that member will serve for a term of three years. Hope’s bill would amend that section of the law to specify that seat for an “individual who was convicted of a felony in this state and served a sentence of not less than 5 years in a department of corrections facility.” “We can’t undo the commission that we have now,” Hope said. “That’s not what this bill is intended to do, but it is intended to cut the reader in bad faith, or the legislator in bad faith, off at the knees if they try to apply it in a way that’s totally contrary to what was ever intended.” She noted during the press conference that she does not expect her bill to pass during the lame duck session that will run through the end of the calendar year. Although Hope herself decided not to seek re-election in 2026 and will be leaving the Legislature at the end of the term, she said that she has spoken with leaders of the incoming Democratic House majority, including caucus chair Rep. Stephanie Young (D-Detroit), who have committed to take up the issue next term. José Burgos, a policy advocate for the Campaign for the Fair Sentencing of Youth who spent 27 years incarcerated in Michigan, expressed hope that the changes would eventually lead to better representation on the commission. “I am very hopeful, very optimistic that at some point the seat that was promised to us will eventually be for somebody with that lived experience to inform that committee on the impact that those sentencing guidelines have on Michigan residents,” he said.

As more ships set out on the Great Lakes, scientists say we need information on the weather they’ll face
articles.description: Data on wind, water and ice conditions are meant to prevent tragedies, but U.S. research cuts, monitoring gaps and climate change put a growing industry at risk.
articles.content: (Damien Gilbert / The Narwhal)The Ontario and federal governments are investing in growing the shipping industry on the Great Lakes. At the same time, climate change is bringing more severe weather conditions. Scientists say investments in climate and weather monitoring need to keep pace with funds for Great Lakes shipping, particularly as cuts have plagued U.S. research under President Donald Trump.That good ship and true was a bone to be chewedWhen the gales of November came earlyThat’s a line from Gordon Lightfoot’s The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald, released 50 years ago. It’s also the story of the SS Edmund Fitzgerald, which sank off the Canadian coast of Lake Superior on Nov. 10, 1975. All 29 crew members died.Scientists say it’s a tragedy that risks repeating itself, as Canada sinks millions of dollars into shoring up Great Lakes shipping without equal investment in weather monitoring and data to ensure safe transit — particularly as climate change brings on more extreme weather and the skies of November turn gloomy.Earlier this fall, the Ontario government announced plans to increase Lake Superior’s commercial shipping capacity by repairing and upgrading Michipicoten Harbour, near Wawa, Ont. Superior Aggregates Corp. received $1 million from the Northern Ontario Heritage Fund to resurrect the harbour, which has not been used by vessels since the 1990s, so it can ship granite and other products to global markets. Northern Economic Development Minister George Pirie said revitalizing the “underused port” can help “reinforce northern Ontario’s role as a competitive gateway” for trade.Farther north on Lake Superior — called Gitchigumi by the Anishinaabe, and in Lightfoot’s song — $2 million in federal funding is going to repurpose unused docks in Marathon, Ont., at the site of a former pulp mill. It will be used to create a terminal for shipping things like forest products and, perhaps someday, critical minerals from the Ring of Fire to southern Ontario and across the globe. The Thunder Bay Port Authority will also receive $800,000 to expand staging and storage capacity at its harbour, so more cargo can flow through the region.But climate change is altering conditions on the lakes. At the same time, cuts to U.S. scientific agencies have raised questions about the quality and future of data used to understand them. That’s data Canadian agencies like Environment and Climate Change Canada use to supplement their own understanding of the state of Great Lakes water.“Great Lakes data is essential infrastructure, just like the locks and the shipping channels are. It requires consistent investment in order to gain the most value and to support extended shipping,” Jennifer Boehme said. She is chief executive officer of the Great Lakes Observing System — an organization that collects and provides public real-time data on wind and water conditions to support storm readiness and ensure safe maritime commerce. “More shipping capacity calls for matching investment and observations.”A huge amount of cargo already moves through the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway, a waterway that allows ships to travel 3,700 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean through the St. Lawrence River to Lake Ontario, including the Hamilton Harbour.Earlier this year, the Lake Carriers’ Association reported that a third of the shipping season was lost because of delays caused by heavy ice. Around the world, weather delays, backlogs and bottlenecks prevent cargo from getting where it needs to go — such as during the infamous 2021 Suez Canal blockage when a sandstorm and strong winds caused a huge container ship to lose control and get stuck, blocking the crucial trade passage for six long days.Inaccurate weather prediction has also already led to disasters. In 2015, the U.S. cargo vessel SS El Faro sank when Hurricane Joaquin swept in near the Bahamas. Reports of the incident show the tropical cyclone updates available to the crew were six hours behind, and that all 33 people on board died.A huge amount of cargo already moves through the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway, a waterway that allows ships to travel 3,700 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean through the St. Lawrence River to Lake Ontario and the other Great Lakes, as far as Lake Superior.Together, these shipments support over $66 billion in economic activity, and 356,858 jobs. However, this August, president of the St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation Jim Athanasiou said the seaway operates at only about 50% of its potential capacity.As the Canadian government invests in expanding its Great Lakes shipping capacity in northern Ontario and beyond, scientists say investments in environment and climate monitoring must keep pace — on both sides of the border.In Canada, weather and climate monitoring on the Great Lakes is done through Environment and Climate Change Canada, by way of federal programs such as the Meteorological Service of Canada and the Canadian Hydrographic Service. The data is shared extensively with the U.S.Currently, Environment Canada has listed “predicting weather and environmental conditions” as one of its core responsibilities for the year, putting $267 million toward forecasts, warnings and data to help Canadians and “weather-sensitive sectors” make decisions. The departmental plan for 2026-2027 promises to do this by monitoring weather, water quantity, ice, air quality and climate conditions and “collaborating closely” with other countries. An independent report produced for the federal environment department last year noted funding for this monitoring has been largely stagnant in Canada for the last five years, “despite increased damages from extreme events.”Getting both Canada and the U.S. on board with Great Lakes weather monitoringSince the Canada-U.S. border bisects four of the Great Lakes, both countries rely on cross-border collaboration and exchange of data to see the full picture.Gail Krantzberg echoes Boehme’s desire for greater investment in data, especially when considering shipping in northern Ontario — an area with harsh winters, heavy snowfalls and violent storms. She’s the Canadian lead investigator at the Global Centre for Climate Change Impacts on Transboundary Waters, a cross-border collaboration between multiple universities and Indigenous nations.“Especially up north, in Lake Superior, if you don’t know ice conditions, how are you going to navigate from port to port? You can’t. It’s too dangerous,” Krantzberg, who is also a professor emeritus at McMaster University, said. “The changing climate is very profoundly changing the Great Lakes. … We need now, more than ever, to better understand how the lakes are functioning.”Krantzberg called U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent cuts to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration “very, very serious,” in an earlier interview with The Narwhal. The organization has lost about 20% of its staff since January 2025, and Krantzberg noted that the Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory’s workforce was cut by about 35 percent.The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration monitors weather, precipitation, winds and ice cover and breakup, “all of which is really critical for the shipping industry to understand, so they can forecast their travels,” Krantzberg said.More cuts are on the table: Trump has proposed to cut the administration’s funding by 26% — or $1.6 billion — for next year’s budget. Industry experts see reason for hope. Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, but many cuts have already been made.On Lake Erie, and other Great Lakes, researchers’ ability to collect observations after freeze-up is limited, as doing it safely requires specialized training and equipment, such as ice-hardened vessels. This creates what experts call a “winter data gap.” Jason Card, vice-president of external affairs at the Ottawa-based Chamber of Maritime Commerce, said there has been strong bipartisan pushback on the cuts. In an email response to The Narwhal’s questions, he pointed to the Great Lakes and National Weather Service Funding Protection Act as an example. Currently in committee in Congress, the legislation seeks to protect National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration funding from being transferred, withheld or reprogrammed without legal justification. “Given this substantive pushback, I believe it would be premature to comment on this matter,” he wrote.Krantzberg said there are limits to how much enhancing Canada’s monitoring capacities can fill the gap left by U.S. partners, especially in the short-term. “It takes a very long time to build up that capacity and huge monetary investments, and our federal government right now is really caught amongst competing priorities,” Krantzberg said. “Buoys and automatic samplers and underwater cameras and all that kind of stuff is major infrastructure.”The Great Lakes ‘winter data gap’In the U.S., the Great Lakes Observing System experienced a close call last spring, when budget cuts proposed by the Trump administration put it at risk of shrinking or vanishing completely. Since then, the organization has been funded through the United States’ National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and was awarded a new five-year co-operative agreement, promising some more certainty for the future, CEO Boehme said.But, important gaps remain.“There are areas where the observations are not as numerous as they should be. There’s room for more information on real-time wind, wave, water level data, currents, ice data,” Boehme said. “Observing capacity needs to grow alongside shipping capacity, not lag behind.”Boehme explained that this information, particularly ice forecasts, are difficult to do in the region because of a lack of year-round observations.This is due to a “winter data gap.” On the Great Lakes, researchers’ ability to collect observations after freeze-up is limited, as doing it safely requires specialized training and equipment, such as ice-hardened vessels. Other equipment, such as the specialized observational buoys Boehme’s organization uses to collect data on the lakes, have to come out of the water before the ice forms. Boehme said that means losing real-time data during some of the “most dangerous months on the lakes when ships are still moving.”Currently, the Great Lakes shipping season runs from late-March to mid-January every year. But, data show, the season has lengthened in the last two decades — gaining an average of 6.5 days annually.More vessels and potentially longer shipping seasons mean more decisions that depend on accurate real-time information.“When shipping runs well into the late fall or early winter storm season, that’s a very critical time,” Boehme said. “Part of the reason that we have buoy monitoring in the Great Lakes is to make sure that Edmund Fitzgerald remains a historical event. November gales are why winter data matters.”

articles.title: FDA Approves First Drug to Treat Neurological Symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher Disease
articles.description: FDA today approved Infilbray (venglustat) tablets, the first treatment for the neurological symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher disease (GD3) in adults and pediatric patients weighing at least 15 kg (approximately 33 pounds).
articles.content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Infilbray (venglustat) tablets, the first treatment for the neurological symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher disease (GD3) in adults and pediatric patients weighing at least 15 kg (approximately 33 pounds). Infilbray crosses the blood-brain barrier to reduce the accumulation of harmful substances in the body and brain. “For patients with Type 3 Gaucher disease, harmful substances build up in the brain without a way to stop them, but this drug's ability to cross the blood-brain barrier means it can get to the source of the buildup driving the neurological symptoms,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “This approval reflects the FDA’s commitment to advancing therapeutic options for patients with rare diseases and brings an important new treatment to patients and the healthcare providers who care for them.” GD3 is a rare, inherited condition in which the body cannot properly break down fatty substances, called glucosphingolipids, due to a deficient or malfunctioning enzyme. As these substances accumulate in organs, tissues, and the brain, patients experience a wide range of serious health problems over time. Unlike type 1 Gaucher disease, GD3 also affects the brain and nervous system, causing difficulties with balance, coordination, speech, memory, and thinking — symptoms that can worsen progressively and significantly impact quality of life. Infilbray works as a glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor, reducing the buildup of harmful substances throughout the body and, critically, within the brain. The FDA’s approval of Infilbray is supported by data from a randomized, double-blind, multicenter clinical study enrolling 43 patients aged 12 years and older with GD3 who had previously been treated with enzyme replacement therapy and had achieved systemic disease stabilization. Participants received either Infilbray orally once daily or intravenous enzyme replacement therapy every two weeks for 52 weeks. Treatment effectiveness was evaluated using two assessments that capture the neurological symptoms central to daily life in patients with GD3, including those related to ataxia (loss of muscle control and coordination) and cognitive function. At Week 52, patients treated with Infilbray demonstrated improvement on a measure that combined both assessments compared to those taking enzyme replacement therapy for the treatment of non-neurologic manifestations of GD3. The most frequently reported side effects of Infilbray include gastrointestinal symptoms as well as adverse effects on mood. Serious psychiatric risks, including suicidal ideation and behavior, have been reported. Potential risks identified from animal studies include potential clouding of vision in younger patients and adverse effects on fetal development when drug is taken during pregnancy. More information on side effects can be found in the drug labeling. Infilbray was granted Orphan Drug designation as well as Priority Review. The approval of Infilbray was granted to Genzyme Corporation, a Sanofi Company. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
articles.description: Measles became endemic in the US months ago—and it's only accelerating.
articles.content: International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings. After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it "shameful" and a "national embarrassment." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases, more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases. There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week. But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What's happening now is a runaway epidemic.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Alaska’s Peltola gives US Senate Dem majority additional cushion
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, which The Associated Press called late Tuesday night, sealed Democrats’ unexpected nine pickups in the midterm elections. Two weeks out from Election Day, the Alaska contest was the last Senate race to be called by The Associated Press. With the flip, Democrats will […]
articles.content: Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Mary Peltola waves to passing motorists on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)WASHINGTON — Former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, which The Associated Press called late Tuesday night, sealed Democrats’ unexpected nine pickups in the midterm elections. Two weeks out from Election Day, the Alaska contest was the last Senate race to be called by The Associated Press. With the flip, Democrats will control 56 seats in the next Congress that begins in January, including two independents who caucus with the party. Peltola held a 12,458-vote advantage over Sullivan as of Wednesday morning, according to AP. In another race that was settled days after polls closed Nov. 3, Democrat Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi was called by the AP on Nov. 11. Colom, a district attorney, narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just over 8,000 votes at the time the race was called. Democrats also flipped Senate seats in the moderate-to-conservative states of Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown also wrested back his Senate seat in Ohio, from Republican Sen. John Husted. Because Brown ran in a special election after Husted replaced Vice President JD Vance, he will be sworn in about two weeks before most other senators elected this month. “Mary Peltola’s victory last night was an exclamation point on what has been a great election year,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters on Capitol Hill Wednesday. “We won because we had great candidates, like Peltola,” Schumer added. “We won because we focused on what the American people cared about: lowering their costs, ending corruption, ending the chaos. But now, you know the American people have given us their votes. Now we have to earn their trust. The real work begins today.” Preliminary results published Tuesday evening by Alaska’s Division of Elections showed Peltola received 50.1% of Alaskans’ first-choice votes, more than enough to avoid a run-off election in the state’s ranked-choice voting system. Scrutinized race The race between Peltola and Sullivan drew scrutiny as Republicans alleged Democrats recruited another candidate with the name Dan Sullivan to run as a spoiler candidate. The two were named on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan, the incumbent senator, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., and the U.S. Justice Department launched a legal challenge in late October to preemptively stop the state from certifying the results of the election if, under the state’s ranked-choice voting system, the Republican incumbent Sullivan lost by a smaller margin than the votes earned by Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher. The New York Times published findings on Oct. 28 that Democratic operatives in Alaska, including in Peltola’s campaign, sought a candidate with the same name. States Newsroom has not independently verified the report. Peltola denied any knowledge of the alleged scheme, according to Alaska Beacon. The Trump administration’s appeal of the case is pending and was amended to reflect the Times’ report. Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy was challenged earlier in the year in state court, and Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled in June he could remain on the ballot. Jennifer Shutt contributed to this report.

articles.title: Environmental groups sue US Forest Service over Upper Peninsula logging plans
articles.description: On Tuesday, a trio of environmental organizations filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Forest Service, arguing its decision to approve a vegetation management project in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula violates the National Environmental Policy Act. In July, the Forest Service announced it would be moving forward with the Silver Branch Vegetation Management Project on the […]
articles.content: Overlook from the Trap Hills within the Ottawa National Forest, Western U.P. in 2021. (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)On Tuesday, a trio of environmental organizations filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Forest Service, arguing its decision to approve a vegetation management project in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula violates the National Environmental Policy Act. In July, the Forest Service announced it would be moving forward with the Silver Branch Vegetation Management Project on the east side of the Ottawa National Forest. According to the agency, the 30-year effort is intended to protect clean water, support wildlife habitats and strengthen recreation opportunities. However, the Upper Peninsula Environmental Coalition, the Environmental Law and Policy Center and the Natural Resources Defense Council argue the Forest Service failed to fully evaluate the environmental impacts of a planned timber harvest that would take place over nearly 80,000 acres of the project area. “A thorough environmental review is part of a proven process that helps ensure that logging on federal lands is done responsibly,” Kelly Thayer, senior policy advocate for the Environmental Law and Policy Center said in a statement Wednesday. “This attempt to bypass the law is part of a series of failed attempts by the Trump administration to streamline operations without considering the consequences. We can make a bigger and better impact on our community by taking reasonable steps to avoid irreversible damage.” Cascade Falls within the Trap Hills, Ottawa National Forest in 2021 (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance) The groups’ also carry concerns beyond the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act. “In authorizing logging on lands the Ottawa has rightly designated as unsuitable for timber harvest, the Forest Service arbitrarily and unlawfully defied the terms of the Ottawa’s own management plan,” the lawsuit states. “And in approving extensive clearcuts that will exacerbate the forest’s significant problems with deer browsing and tree regeneration, the agency violated both the Ottawa’s plan and the National Forest Management Act.” The U.S. Forest Service was asked to comment for this story, but declined, telling Michigan Advance, “it is our practice not to comment on topics of litigation.” While the Forest Service determined the project would have no significant impact on the environment, the environmental groups disagreed. They noted that more than 25,000 acres would be subject to clearcuts, while another 55,000 would be subject to selection harvests, thinning and other forms of logging, which could harm species like the endangered northern long-eared bat. The lawsuit also states that endangered wolves and other wildlife species could be displaced by noise and human presence for up to 10 years. To ensure these resources are adequately protected, the environmental groups have asked the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan to vacate the Forest service’s environmental assessment and decision to approve the Silver Branch project. 5:19 pmA response from the U.S. Forest Service was added to this story.

articles.title: More banks say customers using AI agents are on their own — even if they get hacked
articles.description: Citi is the latest major financial institution to put the breaks on personal finance AI agents.
articles.content: Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked. AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments. But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants. “As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.” JPMorgan and Bank of America, the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eighth largest bank, changed its terms today. Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch. As AI startups look for more revenue, breaking into personal finance presents an attractive opportunity for companies to add value for customers and wet their beaks in the stream of fees generated by the sector. But if consumers are already leery of sharing their email or chat records with an AI agent, bank and brokerage accounts offer a new trust challenge. Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.” Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat. Markets shuddered briefly in reaction to the prospect of AI tools making it easier for consumers to avoid unnecessary fees or low-interest deposit accounts that pad bank margins. But if AI agents become an important way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway. Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability. The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service, and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off. articles.content: Waymo is currently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars' driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times, this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.” This is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations. In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.”Read full article Comments

articles.title: Jeffries chosen to lead US House Dems, poised to be first Black speaker
articles.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. House Democrats voted behind closed doors Wednesday to nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as the party’s leader in the next Congress, teeing him up to become the first Black speaker of the House. Jeffries, a New York Democrat, will come into the 120th Congress with a comfortable majority following the midterm elections, and […]
articles.content: U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks at the Detroit NAACP Fight For Freedom Fund Dinner in Detroit, on April 26, 2026. House Democrats voted Wednesday to make Jeffries their leader in the next Congress. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)WASHINGTON — U.S. House Democrats voted behind closed doors Wednesday to nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as the party’s leader in the next Congress, teeing him up to become the first Black speaker of the House. Jeffries, a New York Democrat, will come into the 120th Congress with a comfortable majority following the midterm elections, and will aim to push through priorities, such as addressing skyrocketing healthcare costs and reining in an aggressive immigration crackdown and war in Iran, amid divided government. “We know millions of people are drowning in this failed Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning things around,” Jeffries told reporters at a press conference following the vote. “Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one: We hear you, we see you, we feel you and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you,” he added. The Associated Press has called 257 House races for Democrats and 171 for Republicans, with seven races not yet called. Democrats voted 251-11 to nominate Jeffries, lawmakers said while exiting the closed door meeting, where cheers could be heard. The support is well above the 218 votes he will need on the House floor in January to become speaker. The House Democratic leadership also includes Rep. Ted Lieu of California as the Democratic Caucus chair, making him the first Asian American to hold that position. Other members of leadership include Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as the Democratic majority leader, poised to become the first woman to take that role in the new Congress. Pete Aguilar of California will be Democratic whip and Joe Neguse of Colorado will be assistant speaker. And Lauren Underwood of Illinois will be the next vice chair for the Democratic Caucus, which would make her the highest-ranking Black woman elected to leadership. While Jeffries will have a Democratic Senate to work with, getting President Donald Trump to sign off on legislation that runs counter to his agenda will be a hurdle. In the weeks since the midterm elections, Jeffries has laid out a handful of priorities for Democrats. At a press conference Tuesday, Jeffries said one of the early pieces of legislation he will bring to the floor is an immigration bill. The measure, known as the American Dream and Promise Act, would provide a pathway to citizenship for people enrolled in Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, and to reissue legal protections for more than 1 million immigrants who were stripped of their Temporary Protected Status by the Trump administration. House Republicans last week voted for Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan to lead them in the minority.

She testified before the panel in September as part of the confirmation process. “Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton,” Cassidy wrote in a social media post. “The (White House) said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate. “My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk. The last issue was that pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues. The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments. Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.” Democrats flipped nine Senate seats in this month’s midterm elections and will hold a 56-44 majority starting in January. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Progress with anti-abortion Republican Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America had encouraged the committee to delay a confirmation vote for Overton, with Senior Vice President of Legal Strategy Erik Baptist writing in a statement released Nov. 11 that “senators must secure commitments from the administration that it will immediately restore the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone and address the serious flaws with the FDA’s mifepristone safety study.” Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley said Tuesday during a brief hallway interview before the White House withdrew Overton’s nomination that he was encouraged by her responses to questions he sent her after the hearing. “I sent her a couple of pages of new questions a few weeks ago, and I just got them back. You know, they’re actually pretty good,” he said. “She commits to finishing the FDA’s mifepristone study by March of 2027. She commits to using all the most recent data. She commits to using private commercial data, including insurer data, where necessary to provide a complete picture, which is something I’ve been pushing for. So, it’s quite a series of commitments. Every commitment I asked her to give, she made.” Hawley added that he didn’t know if the committee would still vote on whether to advance Overton’s nomination several hours before that part of the markup was cancelled. “Your guess is as good as mine,” he said. “I know that there’s building frustration on the committee about the inability of the committee to figure out what it’s doing. My colleagues are getting a little irritated.” Hawley was one of several senators who pressed Overton on her beliefs about medication abortion during the confirmation hearing. Medication abortion a persistent concern The two-pharmaceutical regimen consisting of mifepristone and misoprostol is FDA-approved for up to 10 weeks gestation. It can be prescribed via telehealth and shipped through the mail, a change the FDA made during the Biden administration that many Republicans want to see reversed. The FDA has been conducting its own safety review for much of the last two years. Former Commissioner Marty Makary was forced out of the job in May amid frustration from anti-abortion groups that the agency didn’t plan to release its report ahead of the midterm elections. Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, and Lila Rose, founder of Live Action, both released statements in December pressing for the FDA to restrict access to mifepristone. “The FDA needs a new commissioner who will immediately reinstate in-person dispensing as it existed under President Trump’s first term and immediately conduct a comprehensive study,” Dannenfelser wrote in a statement at the time. “Commissioner Makary is severely undermining President Trump and Vice President Vance’s pro-life credentials and their position that states should have the right to enact and enforce pro-life protections. Makary must go.”

articles.title: Write-In Candidate Scott Farver Nabs Final Seat on East Lansing School Board
articles.description: Two weeks after Election Day, the members of the next school board are set.
articles.content: Two weeks after Election Day, the members of the next East Lansing school board are set, as Scott Farver has won the final seat on the board as a write-in candidate. After three candidates filed by the July deadline to run for four seats on the school board in the Nov. 3 election, a series of write-in candidates joined the field. Farver, a professor in the College of Education at Michigan State University, edged out a victory for the fourth seat on the school board with 699 votes, according to certified totals posted by the Ingham County Clerk’s Office. Community planner Timothy Schmitt received 444 write-in votes and community volunteer services specialist for the American Red Cross Abigail Wright-Geddes received 338 write-in votes. While on-ballot candidates Tali Faris-Hylen, Abbie Tykocki and Delia Fernandez-Jones claimed seats on the board shortly after polls closed on Election Day due to machine counting, write-in candidates are manually verified and counted, which takes more time. According to unofficial results from the Ingham County Clerk’s Office, public relations professional Faris-Hylen and theater business manager Tykocki are returning to the school board, with Faris-Hylen securing 8,183 votes and Tykocki securing 8,392 votes. Delia Fernandez-Jones, a professor of history at Michigan State University, is one of the newcomers to the school board and received the most votes in the race at 8,465, according to unofficial county clerk results. articles.title: Long bus routes from washed-out roads strain some Manistee County schools
articles.description: This story is made possible through a partnership between Interlochen Public Radio and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Some schools in Manistee County have lost students this year because of bus detours from the spring floods, according to district leaders. Key routes remain closed, and one district faces less state funding as a result […]
articles.content: Flooding at Manistee River near Mesick in April. (Vivian La / IPR News)This story is made possible through a partnership between Interlochen Public Radio and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Some schools in Manistee County have lost students this year because of bus detours from the spring floods, according to district leaders. Key routes remain closed, and one district faces less state funding as a result of lower enrollment. “We’re just praying that the road will be reopened prior to next school year,” said Jake Veith, the superintendent of Kaleva Norman Dickson Schools. Veith said the district this year has seen a drop of 46 students. In total, 547 students were enrolled last year. He said families might have decided that school bus detours were simply too long. The daily ride for some students can be two hours round-trip, due to the closure of High Bridge Road in Manistee County. In April, record rainfall swelled rivers across northern Michigan, washing out roads and bridges in parts of the region. The majority of students transferring out of the district — either to other schools or into homeschooling — were from the area of the county hardest hit by the road closures, south of the Manistee River, according to Veith. With a dip in student numbers, the district received $500,000 less in state funding this year. State funding makes up the majority of the district’s typical $7 million to $8 million annual budget. Schools in Michigan receive $10,300 per student in base funding, in addition to state and federal grants. “Financially, it’s hit us big time,” Veith said. “When you only have 500 students in the first place, that’s a lot of students that go directly to your daily operations.” The decreased state funding comes on top of the district’s additional expenses this year for buses, drivers and vehicle maintenance — around $80,000, Veith said. High Bridge Road is still closed, nearly seven months after the initial storms, according to the Manistee County Road Commission. Reconstruction is delayed until spring due to work with federal partners on permitting, including the U.S. Forest Service, which owns the surrounding land. The commission did not respond to IPR’s multiple requests for comment. Record rainfall across parts of northern Michigan last spring pushed regional infrastructure to the brink, including roads, bridges, dams, and even local fish facilities. In nearby Grand Traverse County, the reconstruction of a key thoroughfare is almost complete. Research shows that climate change could fuel more extreme precipitation during the winter and spring transition months, conditions that led to April’s flooding. Veith in Manistee County said the district is not yet in a position where it has to consider layoffs, and he appreciates families sticking with them through these challenges. “We have all of the necessary resources for students and staff to be successful, and we will rebound from this road closure,” he said.

articles.title: Michigan has ignored faulty septic systems for decades. The bill is coming due
articles.description: Only one state lacks a septic code to regulate inspections — and Michigan is paying the price with pollution that routinely sickens thousands.
articles.content: Michigan lacks a statewide septic code, and up to 330,000 systems are failing That has pushed billions of gallons of sewage into Michigan’s 76,000 miles of rivers and streams While other states have cracked down, Michigan legislation is stalled and residents are frustrated After years fixing septic systems in a state that does little to regulate them, it’s hard to gross out Rick Throop. Bridge Listens: See how you can get involved What you should know Fecal-contaminated rivers expose Michiganders who swim, boat, or fish to bacteria, viruses and parasites from sewer overflows, farm runoff and failing septic systems. The contamination likely sickens thousands of people each year and can depress tourism and home values. Who's making public decisions The Michigan Legislature and EGLE hold the key authority over septic rules, farm manure regulation and enforcement, while local municipalities work to make sewer upgrades. Ways to participate Look up your state lawmakers on the state House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee →Contact state representatives who work on the environment. Look up your state lawmakers on the state Senate Energy and Environment Committee →Contact state senators dealing with environmental issues. Attend the Grand Traverse County Board of Public Works meeting →The board meets the second Thursday of the month at Garfield Township Hall, and its verified agenda includes well and water tank inspections, sewer pump station upgrades for several townships, and a state violation notice over a sewage overflow. See the DWSD’s upcoming meetings →The story names the DWSD. We do not list its meetings yet, so check its own schedule for the next one. Look up EGLE water quality reports → What to watch for next Watch whether state lawmakers take up a statewide septic code or stronger manure rules, and whether EGLE's ongoing E. coli testing leads to more waterways being listed as impaired. Are you taking action? Let us know. Submit Thank you! Your response has been recorded. Powered by Civic Action Toolbox But even he recoiled when he arrived at a jobsite to find no septic system at all — just a pipe leading from a waterfront cottage into the St. Clair River near Algonac. “Do me a favor,” he instructed the owner. “Put a wad of toilet paper in your toilet and flush.” Moments later, it was floating downstream. The home was among up to 330,000 statewide with failing or nonexisting septic systems that shunt billions of gallons of sewage annually into Michigan’s rivers, lakes and aquifers. Donate Related: Pure Michigan has a poop problem: Dangerous fecal levels befoul 3 of 4 rivers Along with sewer overflows in cities and manure runoff from farms, failing septics contribute to fecal pollution that makes some 75% of Michigan’s 76,000 miles of rivers and streams unsafe for swimming. The pollution may sicken thousands of people a year. But efforts to fix it fizzle because of sticker shock: One recent estimate put the cost to replace Michigan’s failing septic systems at $2.2 billion or more, a bill that would fall to either taxpayers or individual homeowners at costs that can exceed $15,000 per job. Scientists, public health experts and bipartisan lawmakers blame a regulatory system that too often turns a blind eye to problems. Michigan is the only state in the nation without a uniform septic code. In much of the state, officials don’t even know where all of them are located — much less which ones are failing. Lawmakers have spent a quarter-century talking about the problem but taking little action. Near-annual legislation to bolster oversight has failed amid concerns about logistics, costs and backlash from homeowners who could be forced to make repairs. “Nobody wants to be the bad guy,” said James Lower, a former Republican state representative who joined Democrat Abdullah Hammoud in a failed effort to adopt statewide regulations in 2018. “The consequence, of course, is that there’s quite a bit of sewage going into our groundwater and surface water. It’s just a fact. And it’s unfortunate.” While Michigan languishes, other states in recent years have cracked down. Beginning in February, all septic systems in Washington must be inspected and brought to code when properties are sold, following the lead of states like Ohio and Iowa that have required the inspections for more than a decade. States like Massachusetts go a step further, requiring upgraded systems in environmentally sensitive areas. A deluge of poop Originally devised as a temporary solution for sparsely populated areas of a growing nation, septic systems have instead become permanent fixtures in many rural and suburban communities. Michigan has about 1.3 million, outnumbering all but five states, according to state and US Census Bureau figures. The private disposal systems work by capturing sewage in an underground tank, where solids settle to the bottom and liquids seep into the ground. Under the right circumstances, soil filters bacteria, viruses and nutrients, leaving behind cleaner water. Tanks are meant to be periodically pumped to take care of the rest. Old drain field pipe sits near the pond at Jennifer Kilgore’s home in Attica. When the clogged field stopped draining, the septic tank overflowed and sewage ran toward the water, said Rick Throop, whose crew is replacing the system. (Brayan Gutierrez for Bridge Michigan) But when septic systems fail or are improperly located — say too close to the water table or a shoreline — wastewater leeches into aquifers, lakes and streams.“We have decades of data now that says that’s going to cause water quality problems,” said Joan Rose, a Michigan State University microbiologist whose research has shown human feces is entering waterways near septic systems. Without a statewide code, systems are subject to a patchwork of local regulations that are often so weak they virtually guarantee pollution. Some localities make it legal to build close to shorelines, drinking water wells or the underlying aquifer. While experts recommend drainfields be built 36 inches below the water table, for instance, the bar is lower in 33 Michigan counties, including heavily populated ones such as Macomb and Genesee. Other localities allow systems packed side-by-side on tiny lots, where there isn’t enough soil to absorb all the toilet flushes and laundry loads. And though the average septic system fails after about 30 years, officials in 70 of Michigan’s 83 counties lack inspections to confirm older systems work. Many homeowners don’t even know they own a septic, meaning they likely aren’t keeping up with maintenance. “Failure isn’t always something you can see from the ground surface,” said Sara Heathman, an environmental quality specialist with the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, which has long advocated for a statewide sanitary code that would require periodic inspections. In the handful of Michigan communities that require septic inspections before a home is sold, inspectors have found widespread problems: Pipes shunting human waste directly onto the ground, tanks punctured by tree roots and clogged drainfields located perilously close to a water source. Fearing that septic pollution is harming Higgins Lake’s pristine waters, local public officials enacted a septic inspection ordinance that was later overturned. (Kelly House/Bridge Michigan) Perhaps nowhere were the issues as severe as in Lyon Township, near Higgins Lake in Roscommon County, where a short-lived inspection program revealed health code violations at a majority of residences. The lake is renowned for its crystal blue waters carved by receding glaciers. But failing septic systems and fertilizer runoff are causing algae, odors and declining water quality. “Unfortunately, I think it’s something that’s often out of sight, out of mind,” said Taylor Irwin, environmental health director for the Central Michigan District Health Department, which covers six counties including Roscommon. Faced with the prospect of fixing failing septics or installing public sewers at a cost of $115 million, residents voted to recall most of the township board and elected newcomers who scrapped the inspection program. Similar voter resistance put an end to septic inspections in Barry and Eaton counties. That kind of homeowner backlash also makes lawmakers wary of adopting a statewide septic code that would mandate periodic inspections. The latest proposal, spearheaded by state Sen. Sam Singh, D-East Lansing, has yet to get a floor vote with weeks left in the legislative session. “I appreciate the concept of what we’re trying to achieve: Cleaner water, cleaner Michigan,” said state Sen. Michelle Hoitenga, R-Manton. “I just didn’t feel that there was any way for me to support something that the people I represent were in such opposition to.” The resulting pollution is compounded by a lack of resources to help the poorest Michiganders fix their failing septics. Routine tank pump-outs can cost up to $600, while full system replacement runs $10,000 or more — yet 12% of Americans can’t afford a sudden $400 expense. “Money gets tight … the first thing people are going to look at is, do I put food in the fridge or pump my septic?” said Throop, the repairman. A cleanout at Jennifer Kilgore’s home in Attica gives crews access to the septic system. (Brayan Gutierrez for Bridge Michigan) Lawmakers took a step toward addressing the financial issue in 2024, when they authorized $35 million for a low-interest loan program to help low- and moderate-income Michiganders replace failing septics. The program has helped roughly 475 homeowners. But nearly as many have been rejected because they’re too cash-strapped to qualify for a loan. “It happens quite frequently, and it’s heartbreaking,” said Nishaat Killeen, a programs director with Michigan Saves, the nonprofit that manages the loan program. Grant funding for the neediest homeowners would help fill the gap, Killeen said. But efforts to further boost septic repair funding have gained little traction in Lansing amid strained state budgets and growing anti-tax sentiment. A dozen failed attempts Since the turn of the millennium, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have made more than a dozen attempts to enact a statewide code. Most never got a hearing in Lansing. Lawmakers invariably say they care about cleaning up Michigan’s polluted water. But faced with the pushback from residents who own septic systems, they hesitate to regulate the pollution. “Inaction wins the day,” said Singh. As in past years, Singh’s bill has stalled amid a debate about when — if ever — inspections should be required. Earlier bills called for point-of-sale inspections, but real estate agents objected, citing fears that the discovery of failing systems would slow sales. They advocated instead for periodic inspections at set time intervals. Rick Throop operates an excavator as a coworker checks newly-installed drain field pipes at Jennifer Kilgore’s home in Attica. Tree roots had clogged the home’s old field, so the tank overflowed and sewage surfaced in the yard. (Brayan Gutierrez for Bridge Michigan) Singh’s bill would require systems over 20 years old to be inspected once a decade, with a $50-per-inspection fee to help the state and local health departments administer the program. But lobbying groups representing local governments and public health officials have complained they need more money to launch inspection programs and expressed fear of reprisals from angry homeowners. “It very well could be a safety issue for the inspectors,” said Kevin Green, environmental public health director for the Calhoun County Public Health Department. A more manageable first step, Green said, would be to require inspections only for the highest-risk systems, such as those next to lakes or rivers. Lawmakers could gradually expand oversight, while mapping the state’s septic systems to help local officials enforce existing rules. But

articles.title: Pure Michigan has a poop problem: Dangerous fecal levels befoul 3 of 4 rivers
articles.description: Even as cities spend billions of dollars rehabilitating rivers, Michigan has done a poor job keeping feces out of them. Lawmakers quarrel about solutions as farms and septic systems contaminate the waterways that form the heart of Michigan.
articles.content: An estimated 75% of Michigan’s rivers and streams are tainted with elevated levels of fecal pollution The waste pours off farmland and out of sewers and leaking septic systems, risking the health of swimmers, paddlers and anglers State lawmakers have taken little action amid funding concerns and disagreement about whether Michigan should tighten regulations Rachel Cuschieri-Murray loves the Grand River, which she calls a “precious gift.” The state’s longest river flows 252 miles from Hillsdale County, past farm fields and the state Capitol before emptying into Lake Michigan. But she wouldn’t dare swim in the stretch that flows by those halls of power where lawmakers decide Michigan’s most important issues. “You shouldn’t even put your hands in,” said Cuschieri-Murray, whose duties as executive director of the Eaton Conservation District include caring for the Grand. “It’s that dirty.” Eaton Conservation District leader Rachel Cuschieri-Murray places a sign indicating that stream monitoring is in progress along a 300 foot stretch of Lacey Creek, a Grand River tributary in Eaton County. (Robert Killips for Bridge Michigan) If lakes are the heart of Michigan, its 76,000 miles of rivers and streams are its arteries and pulse, connecting communities, sustaining wildlife and feeding the Great Lakes. Bridge Listens: See how you can get involved What you should know Fecal-contaminated rivers expose Michiganders who swim, boat, or fish to bacteria, viruses and parasites from sewer overflows, farm runoff and failing septic systems. The contamination likely sickens thousands of people each year and can depress tourism and home values. Who's making public decisions The Michigan Legislature and EGLE hold the key authority over septic rules, farm manure regulation and enforcement, while local municipalities work to make sewer upgrades. Ways to participate Look up your state lawmakers on the state House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee →Contact state representatives who work on the environment. Attend the Grand Traverse County Board of Public Works meeting →The board meets the second Thursday of the month at Garfield Township Hall, and its verified agenda includes well and water tank inspections, sewer pump station upgrades for several townships, and a state violation notice over a sewage overflow. Are you taking action? Let us know. Submit Thank you! Your response has been recorded. Powered by Civic Action Toolbox Donate And many are in deep trouble. Despite federal mandates to ease pollution, an estimated 3 in 4 Michigan rivers and streams are so befouled by feces they don’t meet water quality standards meant to keep swimmers and anglers safe. Legislators for years have done little as the problem got worse, fueled by manure runoff from large-scale farms and leaks from tens of thousands of home septic systems. The pollution does more than tarnish the Pure Michigan image. It violates the Clean Water Act and likely sickens thousands of swimmers, boaters and anglers a year from exposure to bacteria, viruses and parasites. “It’s just wild to me that this would be OK,” Michigan Environmental Council Water Policy Director Megan Tinsley said. “And it seems to be OK with a great many of our decision-makers.” Republican and Democratic lawmakers agree pollution is a problem, but disagree on solutions and where it ranks in the state’s long list of priorities. Vegetation covers the water behind a dam on the Pine River in St. Louis, while a sign warns visitors of the E. coli risk. The river is often teeming with bacteria and weeds due to manure pollution from the area’s expanding livestock industry. (Kelly House/Bridge Michigan) Related: Michigan has ignored faulty septic systems for decades. The bill is coming due While environmental groups think state manure pollution regulations are too lax, the livestock industry has sued to block their enforcement. Money remains a perpetual obstacle, preventing cities from making repairs to leaky sewers and stopping lawmakers from requiring people to fix their failing septic systems. The inaction threatens to undermine investments taxpayers have made to reclaim Michigan’s rivers, including billions spent to dredge contaminated sediment, restore habitat and replace derelict factories with waterfront parks. “Ultimately, a polluted environment is not going to allow for economic growth and it’s not going to allow for health and wellness,” said Joan Rose, a Michigan State University microbiologist who has extensively studied the problem. Awash in waste The more regulators look for fecal waste in the water, the more they find. The state has so far tested roughly half of Michigan’s rivers and tributaries for E. coli, a gut bacteria regulated under the Clean Water Act as a proxy for fecal contamination. The Blue Bridge stretches across the Grand River in Grand Rapids. (Ella Miller/Bridge Michigan) The vast majority exceeded levels deemed safe for swimming. In more than half, levels are often too high even for even partial body contact activities, like paddling or wading. Based on results so far, an estimated 75% of Michigan’s rivers and streams likely exceed state limits for fecal contamination, said Molly Rippke, who leads E. coli testing for the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy. That doesn’t necessarily mean they’re always polluted. Water quality fluctuates over time and most waterways aren’t routinely sampled. Still, Rippke said the numbers do “not look pretty.” How much is too much? Michigan attempts to protect public health by limiting the number of allowable E. coli per 100 milliliters of water (just under a half cup). The state limits are: Full-body swimming: No more than 300 E. coli at any given time, and a mean of no more than 130 E. coli across multiple samples during a 30-day period Partial-body contact (paddling, wading, fishing): No more than 1,000 E. coli at any given time The pollution spans the state, from small creeks to parts of major rivers like northern Michigan’s Boardman and Pere Marquette, mid-Michigan’s Tobacco, southwest Michigan’s Kalamazoo and the Rouge in metro Detroit. The risks extend to the state’s lakes, causing bacteria-related closures or advisories at dozens of beaches every summer. It’s difficult to directly compare Michigan to its neighbors, because states vary in monitoring and levels of bacteria deemed unsafe. But fecal pollution is widespread. In Indiana, 74% of assessed river miles exceed regulatory limits. In Illinois, the figure is 83%. Nationally, a recent study from Environment America found elevated bacteria levels at 69% of monitoring locations across 17 states. The situation frustrates river lovers like AJ MacArthur, a Kalamazoo resident who founded the paddling club Michigan River Rats. He blames a culture of environmental neglect that also fuels the PFAS crisis and littering. “It’s just beyond me,” MacAthur said. “We’re supposed to be known for our water.” A young angler baits a line along the Pine River in Alma. Elevated levels of E. coli in the river make it risky to touch the water or even the fish without washing hands. (Kelly House/Bridge Michigan) The dirtiest waterways tend to be small tributaries in the southern half of the Mitten, where livestock farms, failing septic systems and sewage dumping cause widespread problems. Among them: the White River in the Thumb, the north branch of the Salt River near Coleman, the Red Run drain in Warren and various tributaries of the Flint, Grand and Raisin rivers. As those tributaries flow into bigger rivers, the waste gets diluted — but not always enough to eliminate health risks. Goose droppings, dog waste and sewer overflows add to the toll as rivers wend through suburbs and cities. “We don’t have a whole lot of choice other than be reactionary,” Flint Environmental Compliance Supervisor Tiffany Minder said of the city’s struggles with sewer backups during rainstorms. “Our infrastructure is 100 years old.” Disgusting and dangerous More than just gross, waste-laden water is dangerous. Accidentally swallowing it can expose a person to a long list of pathogens, from E. coli and cryptosporidia to norovirus, giardia and hepatitis. Fever, diarrhea and vomiting are the most common symptoms, but some infections spiral into severe illness or lasting organ damage. “We’re really just beginning to break the ice on what the long-term consequences of those infections are,” said Dr. James M Fleckenstein, a Washington University School of Medicine professor who studies E. coli. “But generally, we know that contaminated water is not a good thing.” When met, Michigan’s water quality standards are supposed to limit the number of people sickened to a handful out of every 1,000 swimmers. The greater the exceedance, the greater the risk. Is my river safe? Click the link below to view a map of tested waterways. Zoom in on your community to see test results. View the map State statistics show at least 12.4 million people spend time on Michigan’s rivers and 30.7 million swim at the state’s beaches each year, but nobody tracks how many are sickened by fecal pathogens during the experience. People usually fight off the resulting stomach bugs at home, Fleckenstein said, perhaps wrongly blaming food poisoning or a seasonal illness. However, estimates from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggest the nationwide toll could top a million. A separate study, from researchers at the University of Illinois and Indiana University, reached a far higher estimate of 50 million annual gastrointestinal illnesses associated with lakes, rivers and ocean beaches. As the 10th most populous state and a place known for its water, Michigan likely has a higher percentage, said Matthew Sims, a physician researcher specializing in infectious diseases at Corewell Health. Sims and his colleagues see patients with signs of such illnesses “all the time.” “If somebody says we went camping, if somebody says we drank stream water, river water, whatever: We know there’s potential issues,” Sims said. Beyond harboring disease, fecal pollution can overload the water with nutrients that cause toxic algae blooms and oxygen-depleted dead zones where fish can’t survive. It inflicts an economic toll in the form of missed workdays, medical bills, reduced tourism and depressed real-estate values. One Michigan-based study found waterborne E. coli outbreaks diminished home prices by an average of $13,000 when a sale coincided with an outbreak. “Why would people want to continue to come here if over half of our waters are out of compliance for swimming?” said Tinsley, the Michigan Environmental Council water advocate. MacArthur, the Kalamazoo paddler, follows a strict routine to minimize his exposure: No swimming. Wear rubber boots when launching or landing. Keep your hands away from your mouth. Shower immediately upon returning home. “There are ways around it,” he said of the health risks. “But it’s unfortunate that we have to even think about that.” Anglers on the bank of the Kalamazoo River in Battle Creek. A section of the river, in downtown, flows through a concrete channel to control flooding. (Josh Boland/Bridge Michigan) Lawmakers agree on problem, not solutions Legislative leaders on both sides of the aisle call the pollution unacceptable for a state so rich in water resources. But they are split on how to address it and have focused little attention to doing so in recent ye
