The popular bipartisan proposal has been on Congress’ to-do list for years and is a top priority for the 120th Congress, according to Democrats who will assume the majority in […]
articles.content: Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, who flipped Michigan’s 7th Congressional District from Republican to Democrat, spoke against congressional stock trading on Capitol Hill on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Current and incoming Democratic U.S. House members demanded a ban Tuesday on congressional stock trading starting on day one of the new Congress. The popular bipartisan proposal has been on Congress’ to-do list for years and is a top priority for the 120th Congress, according to Democrats who will assume the majority in January. “To me, it’s such a commonsense issue,” Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., said during a press conference on Capitol Hill. “Members of Congress should not be allowed to enrich themselves by trading stocks,” she added. “As part of our job, many of us have access to information the rest of the world does not. Using that information for profit is called insider trading, and for any other person, it would be illegal. Members of Congress should not get to play by different rules.” Grijalva, Reps. Jason Crow, D-Colo., Chris Deluzio, D-Pa., and Primila Jayapal, D-Wash., led the event alongside just over a dozen newly elected Democrats including former mayors, a labor leader and an attorney who represented children in foster care. “I ran because I got tired of seeing my patients being unable to afford their medications … all while seeing our member of Congress here in this building enriching himself,” said Rep.-elect Mitchell Berman, an emergency room nurse who beat Republican incumbent Rep. Bryan Steil of Wisconsin. Steil nearly doubled his net worth while in Congress to $1.9 million, according to an analysis by Wisconsin Watch, a nonprofit investigative news organization. Steil was the main sponsor of a recent U.S. House-passed stock trading ban bill. Senate Democrats blocked that legislation, citing loopholes they said allowed members to continue owning stocks and excluded the president from restrictions. The bill was also attached to a voter ID measure. Steil’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. $2.1B of trades in 3 years Members of Congress executed nearly 36,000 trades in the past three years, totaling over $2.1 billion, according to the anti-corruption and government reform advocacy groups Public Integrity Project and P Street, which both supported the press conference. Nearly 60 incoming freshmen have signed a pledge with the Public Integrity Project, vowing to ban congressional stock trading, reject corporate political action money, abstain from lobbying after leaving Congress and overturn Citizens United, according to the advocacy organization. And more than 50 newly elected Democrats sent a letter last week urging Democratic leadership to instate a rule on the first day of the 120th Congress banning members of the House from trading stocks. Other incoming Democrats who spoke Tuesday included Reps.-elect Matt Little of Minnesota, Katy Padilla Stout of Texas, Will Lawrence of Michigan, Brad Lander of New York, Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania, Cyril Jefferson of North Carolina, Zach Dembo of Kentucky and Lindsay James of Iowa. Democrat Jake Johnson, D-Minn., also spoke, though The Associated Press has not officially called his race against incumbent Republican Rep. Brand Finstad.

articles.title: States struggle to impose new Medicaid work rules, even with 6-month reprieve
articles.description: Last week the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services extended the deadline by six months to June 30, 2027, for state Medicaid programs to impose work requirements on their enrollees, but states still face a slew of unique challenges keeping people on the rolls. Among the many logistical challenges states are figuring out are […]
articles.content: Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, speaks at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington, D.C., in December 2025. Despite a six-month reprieve, many states will struggle to implement new Medicaid work requirement rules. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)Last week the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services extended the deadline by six months to June 30, 2027, for state Medicaid programs to impose work requirements on their enrollees, but states still face a slew of unique challenges keeping people on the rolls. Among the many logistical challenges states are figuring out are how to communicate the many different exceptions to enrollees for work rules, overhauling their eligibility systems to have people seamlessly turn in their paperwork to verify income and hiring more staff to review those documents. Last week, after months of hearing from state Medicaid programs that meeting the former Jan. 1 deadline would be too challenging and expensive, Daniel Brillman, CMS’s deputy administrator and director, offered states in a Nov. 13 letter a reprieve, which he called a “hold harmless” period, offering states another six months without penalty. Still, some states, such as Montana and Nebraska, rolled out their work requirements early and have already hit some road bumps. Jeremy Nordquist, president and CEO of the Nebraska Hospital Association representing the state’s hospitals, said he’s been working with the state to reach Medicaid enrollees and noticed that the biggest barrier has been communication. “It’s really important to try to get down, you know, as deep into the community as possible. Typically these folks aren’t watching local news as much as the general population. They’re not following healthcare policy,” Nordquist said. According to Nebraska state data, by August 2026, around four months after the state began enforcing work rules on May 1, the state had already denied 557 new Medicaid applicants due to the new requirements. But among those the vast majority — 466, or 83.7% — had simply failed to provide documentation needed to prove compliance or an exemption from the rules. Another 533 people who were renewing their Medicaid were also denied. Of those, 490, or 91.9%, also failed to provide documentation. Overall that meant at least 956 people lost their Medicaid because of paperwork, which many experts have said would be the biggest challenge. “Early on, we saw the state send a letter to Medicaid recipients with a high-level overview of what would be needed, and it was really written at a 14th-grade reading level,” Nordquist said. “That’s really not something that’s easily comprehensible or easily followed up on by Medicaid populations.” And in Montana, Dr. Aaron Wernham, CEO of the Montana Healthcare Foundation, a healthcare policy and investment group, said even before work requirements in the state, it was already hard to get enrollees help if they were struggling with paperwork. “We have long wait times in the Medicaid call center, high rates of call abandonment by people trying to call in to get help and also very high rates — among the nation’s highest — of renewal applications taking more than 45 days to process, that was before all the work requirement stuff,” Wernham said. Different states, different problems Every state is dealing with its own set of circumstances, and so are enrollees. Federal work requirements state that adults under the age of 64 and who are able-bodied earning up to 138% of the federal poverty line (around $22,000 for an individual) would have to volunteer, go to school or work for at least 80 hours a month or meet a minimum household income of $580 a month ($6,960 for a household year) in order to be eligible for Medicaid. But among the 41 states plus the District of Columbia that expanded Medicaid to adults with lower incomes, as well as those that partially expanded through waivers such as Georgia, Tennessee and Wisconsin, 31 have minimum wages that are higher than the federal government’s minimum wage of $7.25 and would have to work fewer than 80 hours. And across 20 states plus D.C., enrollees are eligible for Medicaid if one person in their household works at least 40 hours a month. So, each state will have to consider its own minimum wage standards every year while calculating enrollees’ eligibility. Many states shift their minimum wages every year. Quotation It's just an additional administrative burden, not only on the Medicaid agencies, but also on providers who have to chime in to help. – Jennifer Evans, an attorney at Polsinelli working with healthcare providers and former Medicaid director for Colorado “They might be checking if they have pay stubs or other data sources that might show hours worked or connections with education hubs to see education status,” said Amaya Diana, a health policy analyst at health research group KFF. “And then, if they don’t have data on file, that’s where they may ask for additional documentation from an enrollee, and that is where they might be submitting extra documents to the state.” Given that enrollees can meet the requirements or seek an exemption in many different ways, Rebecca Kellenberg, a principal at Health Management Associates, a firm that helps organizations implement health policy, said states will have to really focus on their communication strategies so enrollees don’t think they are unqualified when they actually are. “I think states are anticipating that the majority are already working or will meet some exclusions based on their circumstances, and that the challenge is documenting that work,” Kellenberg said. “It’s a communication challenge to figure out what the documentation requirements are … that will be the biggest challenge for ensuring individuals don’t lose coverage when they are in fact eligible and meeting requirements.” In Nebraska, Nordquist said his biggest takeaway for states and hospitals is to start early. “We created Spanish language resources that our hospitals could use in their communities doing outreach to try to explain the requirements that were coming but also make sure to tell people to keep their information current,” Nordquist said. “This Medicaid expansion population tends to move more frequently than the general population, so physical mail isn’t always the best. “That’s why it’s so important we find ways to break down those barriers and get people’s contact information updated as frequently as possible.” Most enrollees already working Most people on Medicaid are already working, and states already check income for Medicaid eligibility. While meeting a smaller standard of just 40 hours or less may not be a challenge for many, the paperwork of providing proof of income twice a year will be the actual significant and unnecessary burden to people who are working, said Jennifer Evans, an attorney at Polsinelli working with healthcare providers and former Medicaid director for Colorado. Data from KFF shows 63% of adults on Medicaid work 80 hours a month or attend school. “It’s just that they don’t make enough money, or they don’t work in a location that offers health insurance. … These are low-wage earners, and so I don’t think that the fact that the dollar number is less is going to have a material impact,” Evans said. “It’s just an additional administrative burden, not only on the Medicaid agencies, but also on providers who have to chime in to help.” In Washington, D.C., for example, the Medicaid program will have to distinguish between District workers and federal workers. While people under federal law minimally earn $7.25 per hour, District workers earn $18.40 per hour, almost three times as much. “The biggest challenge will be ensuring that District residents are reporting all their income so that DHCF (Department of Health Care Finance) can accurately determine their total income and subsequently, their compliance with the work requirements,” Melisa Byrd, senior deputy director of D.C.’s Medicaid program, wrote to Stateline. “DHCF’s goal is to utilize electronic sources for income verification whenever possible — but we will accept any other documentation showing earned income.” Byrd wrote that the department estimates that of the approximately 75,000 Medicaid adult enrollees without children who would be subject to work requirements, nearly a third appear compliant based on their household income of at least $580 in a month. That means states and municipalities will still face a host of challenges keeping Medicaid recipients on the rolls who may be working inconsistently, facing unemployment or dealing with unforeseeable circumstances. “Many people on Medicaid have little to no income, and little to no taxable income,” said Jennifer Wagner, director of Medicaid eligibility and enrollment at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan policy research group. “Many people turn to Medicaid in a time of crisis, such as when they’ve lost a job and are in between jobs, or they’ve had a medical crisis that’s caused them to take time off of work,” Wagner said. “Their annual income might be higher, but when they apply for Medicaid, they may be very low income.” Wagner said states will face confusion and paperwork issues around people who are in school, medically frail, caregivers, or fall under other exclusions. Enrollees taking care of kids under the age of 14 are also exempt from the work rules. In June, 25 Democratic-led states plus the District of Columbia sued the Trump administration over the work requirement, largely on the basis of their decision to change “medically frail” guidelines to ask enrollees to prove they are too sick to work. In late October, a U.S. district judge struck down that part of the rule, saying it would cause significant harm to enrollees and create costs for states, but granted some concessions to the federal government in other areas. Specifically, the court upheld the federal government’s new rule requiring that states look back at 12 months of claims data to determine whether an enrollee meets the medical frailty exemption at all. States also have to look back at least a month at an enrollee’s work history for them to apply at all. In the past, states did not have to do this, Wagner said. According to KFF, right now 31 states have opted to look back one month to determine eligibility, but five states plan to look back two to three months. Another two will look back three months after a quarterly compliance check. “This idea of looking back at a month instead of what your current circumstances are is not a concept in Medicaid,” Wagner said. “It’s not the way applications are structured. It’s not the way eligibility systems are structured, and so this is a totally new thing.” Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org. articles.title: What is a vector database? How AI search finds meaning
articles.description: Learn what a vector database is, how it works, and where it’s used. See examples, types, and how it compares to relational and graph databases.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. A vector database is a storage system that allows AI models to query and retrieve unstructured data based on semantic similarity. It helps AI generate responses with knowledge beyond its training data. Vector databases store the information in a format that LLMs can process easily. They provide AI models with additional information to generate relevant and accurate answers. This guide explains what a vector database is, how it works, common use cases, types, examples, and how it compares to relational and graph databases. A vector database stores data as numerical representations called embeddings, enabling low-latency semantic search for AI models. Unlike a traditional database, which stores information in rows and columns, a vector DB clusters embeddings in a multidimensional space based on semantic similarities. In AI, the term ‘dimension’ describes learned features or characteristics of a specific object. For example, you can picture a dog as having dimensions such as fur color and breed. In practice, individual dimensions in a learned embedding rarely map to one readable feature. Generative AI applications, particularly those that connect to an external knowledge source, use a vector database to expedite retrieval. Instead of searching for a direct keyword match in a traditional database, the retriever system finds the most similar embeddings in the vector DB. Let’s say a customer called and asked you to recommend a “blue sweater”. With a traditional database, you look for products that match the attributes “blue” and “sweater”. However, if the customer wants “outfits that feel comfortable for a long flight”, a traditional database couldn’t return an answer. Meanwhile, a vector database captures the request's semantic meaning. By mapping it to the vector space, the system returns outfits like sweatpants, hoodies, and travel pillows, which have closely related feature representations. This ability to match meaning is what sets a vector DB apart from a traditional one. Vector embeddings are arrays of numbers that represent unstructured data like text, images, and video so AI models can process it easily. A vector is the mathematical representation of numbers across different dimensions. However, a vector doesn’t capture the context, structure, and meaning of a specific dataset. For example, a list of floating numbers [0.82, 0.14, 0.67] is a vector, but what it represents is determined by the embedding model. Embeddings capture qualities of the data and store them as a vector in a multi-dimensional space. They give meaning to what would otherwise be just a list of numbers. Each number in the vector is one dimension of the learned representation. Let’s say you want to store customer cases in a vector DB. Using an embedding model, you convert ticket types into embeddings with distinct values across dimensions. The values below are simplified for illustration. Refund delay beyond expected processing time Unable to access account due to login failure Both refund issues, despite different causes, have higher numbers in the first and second dimensions, while the login issue has its highest number in the third. Embedding models typically produce hundreds or thousands of dimensions, which is why vector databases are built to compare them quickly. Vector databases turn unstructured data into embeddings, store them in a multidimensional space, and facilitate semantic similarity search. Embeddings that are closely linked to each other will, to an extent, have a smaller distance in the vector space. When the vector database receives a query, it uses approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms to retrieve the most similar embeddings without scanning the entire database. These are stages for setting up and retrieving from a vector database. First, an embedding model converts unstructured data into embeddings. Each embedding represents features that carry semantic meaning of the real-world object. Then, the system stores the embeddings, along with the original data and metadata, into the vector DB. Because embeddings with similar meaning sit close together in the vector space, the database can retrieve relevant matches by measuring the distance between vectors. Indexing is a process that organizes the vector embeddings to improve retrieval efficiency. Vector databases use several indexing techniques to group closely related embeddings. For example, a vector DB may use a list, graph, or tree structure, depending on the retrieval requirements. Besides indexing, the vector DB might compress the data using a technique called product quantization. Product quantization compresses embeddings into compact codes, which saves memory at the cost of a small loss in search accuracy. When receiving a query, the vector database turns it into an embedding. Then, it compares the query’s embedding with those stored in the vector’s multi-dimensional database using techniques like cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance. Based on the results, the vector database returns embeddings with the closest semantic similarity score, which generative AI applications use to augment their answers. Together, storage, indexing, and querying let the database return relevant results quickly. Similarity search is a broad category of information matching systems. It includes keyword-based approaches that match the exact words in a query, as well as vector search, which matches on meaning. Vector search uses a vector database to return semantically related answers. Instead of performing an exact keyword search, vector search compares the distance between the query and answer candidates to choose the most appropriate result. Often, the vector DB uses metadata to pre-filter the embeddings before running a similarity search. For example, it narrows down the search by filtering embeddings within a specific time frame. This way, retrieval is faster. Vector databases help customer support teams deploy voice AI and chatbots that can respond with accurate product knowledge. In an AI-powered customer support system, the vector database stores proprietary knowledge bases such as product guides, business policies, and customer cases. The AI agent connects to the vector DB using a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. When the AI voice agent receives a query, it checks if it has sufficient information to answer the customer. If it lacks current or sufficient data, the RAG retrieves semantically matching data to augment the answer. Let’s say a voice agent receives the following complaint: “My blender won’t spin after two weeks. Can I get my money back?” Instead of searching for exact keywords like “won’t spin” and “money back," the RAG turns the request into an embedding. Then, it retrieves refund policies that share the closest meaning. By retrieving relevant internal documents, a RAG system backed by a vector database helps reduce hallucinations in voice agents, although it does not eliminate them. Instead of guessing, both AI and human agents can use internal documents to resolve customer queries. A relational database uses rows and columns, alongside a fixed schema, to store its data. A vector DB instead uses embeddings, which represent unstructured data. Relational databases suit exact matches and structured queries, such as finding every order placed on a given date. On the other hand, vector databases retrieve the stored embeddings closest in meaning to a query, which is more effective for natural language questions. Most of the time, teams will use both, as they both have their place when working with data. Graph databases use knowledge graphs to connect different entities in ways that reflect their hierarchy and relationships. AI systems like GraphRAG use graph databases to answer queries that need multi-hop reasoning. When you query a graph database, it finds the starting data point and uses a graph traversal algorithm to find related entities. For example, customer names can link to renewal dates and support tickets in sequence. Meanwhile, vector databases store unstructured data with numerical representations based on their semantic meaning. They let RAG systems perform simple query matching at very low latency. For example, a vector DB surfaces the refund policy when processing “I want a refund." Both vector and graph databases offer utility to AI systems. You can use both of them together: Generally, there are two types of vector databases, differentiated by their architectural style. The choice between them mainly rests on whether you need a dedicated system for large query workloads or instead want a semantic search element in a database you are already running. Which one fits depends on your scale and how much infrastructure you want to manage. ElevenAgents lets voice agents retrieve from your own knowledge base to enable conversational, context-aware responses. By using RAG, the agent retrieves the most semantically similar content from the documents, URLs, or text you add to the knowledge base. You can set retrieval to “On demand” so the agent searches the knowledge base only when it decides it needs to. Understandably, implementing RAG increases response-generation latency. However, thanks to our engineering advancements, we reduced ElevenAgents' RAG median latency from 326ms to 155ms. Get started with ElevenAgents and learn how to set up your knowledge base here. Vector databases include standalone databases and integrated vector capabilities. Standalone vector DB are purpose-built for end-to-end vector operations. Meanwhile, databases with integrated vector capabilities support semantic similarity search while maintaining existing data architecture. Vector embeddings represent real-world data as numbers so AI systems can compare it by meaning. They support semantic similarity search and RAG-based systems, where the system retrieves data based on conceptual relevance and uses it to ground its answers. Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant, and Chroma are examples of standalone vector databases. PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension and MongoDB Atlas Vector Search are examples of existing databases with vector capabilities. In a voice agent, a vector DB might store a company's refund policies and return the closest match when a customer asks about a refund. MongoDB is a general-purpose document database that supports vector search through MongoDB Atlas Vector Search, which stores embeddings alongside documents and queries them by similarity. That places it in the vector DB extension category. ElevenAgents includes a knowledge base that lets voice agents answer questions from your own documents using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The agent converts each question into a vector embedding and retrieves the most semantically similar content from your knowledge base. You can run retrieval on every turn, only when the agent decides it needs it, or turn it off, and you can configure the embedding model, vector distance limit, and number of candidates under semantic search. Learn more in the ElevenAgents RAG documentation. A vector has a different meaning in different research fields. In maths, a vector refers to a quantity that has a direction and magnitude. In biology, meanwhile, a vector refers to a vehicle that carries DNA to a target cell. Agents can now use Scribe v3 Live Medical, our first real-time medical transcription for agents, to accurately transcribe clinical language as people speak. articles.title: Mod Pods pushed back again as city makes new winter shelter plans
articles.description: It has been just over a year since Lansing bought 50 modular housing units, better known as Mod Pods, to try to help the ongoing struggle of the estimated thousands […]
articles.content: It has been just over a year since Lansing bought 50 modular housing units, better known as Mod Pods, to try to help the ongoing struggle of the estimated thousands who are experiencing homelessness in Lansing. Then-HRCS Deputy Director Delvata Moses said the pods would house 66 residents experiencing homelessness and help them transition to permanent housing. Interiors of the NOVA Housing Initiative/Mod Pod units, on display at Lansing City Hall this summer. Lieza Klemm/City Pulse Initially, HRCS aimed to break ground in March 2026 and open operations for the pods in June if “all goes well.” Then-HRCS Director Kimberly Coleman told City Pulse in August 2025 that the purchase was made somewhat rapidly. “Because the purchase was time-sensitive, we moved quickly to address an urgent need,” she said at the time. “That speed came at the expense of upfront planning in some areas,” Coleman said, and that department would create a plan with “clear milestones.” City Council approved the request for $640,000 for 50 modular housing units from Kalamazoo-based Housing Resources Inc. (HRI); the vote was met with largely public approval for the project. HRI had put the pods up for sale after canceling its own transitional housing project. The nonprofit, which connects Kalamazoo County residents with housing resources, hit several snags when trying to find a potential location for the pods. Lansing city officials believed they had sidestepped that problem by looking at city-owned property for the pod sites. Kim Coleman, left, and other officials with Lansing’s NOVA Housing Initiative (Mod Pods) during a public meeting in August. Lieza Klemm/City Pulse Coleman retired as director in February and now leads the project for the city. In a July meeting with city council members, Coleman described the difficulties of the project in a July meeting with City Council members, saying, “we had really grandiose ideas.” In a late August meeting with the public, officials with the Nova project said they had finally been able to hire a construction manager. The manager was needed to create a site plan and a timeline. In November, council members were told that the priorities were shifting to a low-barrier winter shelter, with the Mod Pods being pushed off for another winter. A year and some change later, the timeline for the urgent project is as clear as mud. Paved lot instead of park Over several months and numerous community meetings, the original supportive response from Lansing residents shifted into an onslaught of critiques, ranging from the plan’s development to site proposals for the pods. After narrowing down 48 possible locations, the city presented five finalists to the public: Comstock Park, Hunter Park, Reasoner Park, the former warming house in Debbie Stabenow Park and the former Shabazz Academy. Joan Nelson, the retired founding director of the Allen Neighborhood Center, spoke at a December 2025 meeting about the Mod Pod community. Leo V. Kaplan/City Pulse Then the city completely switched course. In January of this year, two advisory boards recommended the Ingham County Health and Human Services parking lot for the pods. Lansing Mayor Andy Schor supported their choice. In the midst of the city deciding where to put the pods, leadership at HRCS changed. Coleman resigned, and Moses was named as interim director. In a statement announcing her resignation, Schor said Coleman would continue to work on the transitional housing project. A Request for Proposal went out to find an organization to handle daily operations and case management for the initiative. In July, city officials announced that Detroit Rescue Mission Ministries (DRMM), the proposal’s only applicant, would run the Mod Pod community. The annual cost of daily maintenance of the pods – including restrooms, laundry facilities, a community room, meeting and training spaces, 24/7 security and “resident empowerment programming” – is estimated at $952,335, roughly $14,400 per person. The city set aside about $1.9 million for site preparation and construction. Interiors of the NOVA Housing Initiative/Mod Pod units, on display at Lansing City Hall this summer. Lieza Klemm/City Pulse The most recent community meeting was in August. Representatives from DRMM, HRCS, the architect and construction companies updated residents on the project’s status. HRCS’s former director Coleman was also present as a “transitional housing and homelessness strategy consultant.” The meeting marked progress on the project; a construction manager had finally been hired after two unsuccessful rounds. But given the pods’ purpose and the designated location, which had moved from the county building’s east lot to the west, nothing about the project was standardized. Shantel Spears, a formerly homeless resident, spoke during a January meeting in support of the parking lot proposal. Leo V. Kaplan/City Pulse During the meeting, Clark Construction Company President Robert LaLonde said they had trouble finding a building code to assign the project, forcing the company to consider “doing it under a different kind of campground code.” The construction firm is the project’s general contractor. Long-term funding sources and the potential burden on taxpayers to keep the project running remain up in the air. Coleman said in August that similar programs rely on a mix of private, public, and federal funding, and the city’s initiative will “be doing the same.” HRCS has not provided a construction progress for the community or City Council since that August meeting. Shifting priorities Last week, HRCS Interim Director Moses brought a report to the Lansing City Council to update officials on “homelessness efforts.” Moses told council members that while the department is not switching gears entirely, priorities are changing from Mod Pods to an emergency drop-in center. The priority now is setting up an “emergency” low-barrier, overnight drop-in center, meant to be open during the winter months, then focus on establishing a permanent center. “The emergency overnight center addressed the immediate gaps,” Moses said. “So, our top priority right now is getting the low-barrier drop-in center up and running to address the current street and winter conditions, which require an immediate response.” The center will be open daily from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m. Moses said the department is working to open a center at Union Baptist Church as an alternative for families with minor children. The Lansing Planning Commission and City Council are expected to review the necessary zoning changes and permits for the temporary drop-in center next month. HRCS general funds, a portion of the City’s 2025 opioid crisis settlement and $100,000 from Ingham County’s housing and homeless millage will fund the temporary drop-in center. ‘Not just stringing us along’ Five months have passed since the Mod Pod project’s original anticipated opening date. Moses said the units will be operational “sometime next year.” Councilmember Deyanria Nevarez Martinez said it was troubling to hear the project was delayed once again. “The last update we had gave us an impression of something that’s obviously not happening,” she said. “These updates need to actually have outcomes, not just stringing us along on something that’s actually been very expensive and will continue to be very expensive for our city.” Interiors of the NOVA Housing Initiative/Mod Pod units, on display at Lansing City Hall this summer. Lieza Klemm/City Pulse Mayor Andy Schor said the construction crew was seeing “significant issues that are involved,” including site leveling, hooking up utilities and building a permanent shelter for extreme weather conditions. “The pods will continue, but we have to navigate funding,” he said. “We want to get folks off the street … but there are limited resources.” The temporary drop-in center presented to Lansing City Council has been in the works for months, according to city spokesperson Scott Bean. The first group chosen to operate a “Cold Blue” emergency center dropped out at the last minute, and the city pivoted. “We went kind of hardcore, full speed ahead on, ‘Let’s do this seven days a week, every night through the winter, not just Code Blue nights,’” he said. The center will be in the former Salvation Army building off of Pennsylvania Ave., and will include 70 beds. Detroit Rescue Mission Ministries will be operating the center, Bean told City Pulse. Continued delays According to Ingham County Commissioner Chair Ryan Sebolt, there are options on the table for saving money, as a trade-off instead of opening sooner. The county is building a new juvenile detention center, with construction supposed to start next year. When the new facility is finished and the old one is emptied, the NOVA Housing Initiative could use the old center as a site. Developers of Lansing’s NOVA Housing Initiative (Mod Pods) met in August with community members and gave an update on the project. Lieza Klemm/City Pulse Sebolt said it would eliminate a significant number of the issues the construction contractor is encountering. “There would be no utility hookup that’s needed because it’s already hooked up,” he said. “There’d be no need to build other structures to facilitate the pods because we can use the building that already exists. So we can actually take that off the price tag and present considerable savings on building, and then have more money for services if we delay.” Waiting for construction of the new facility to finish would mean delaying opening the pods until 2028, if not later. Sebolt told City Pulse he “threw that option out” to Mayor Schor and other staff members involved in the project, but the city is “really in the driver’s seat on this.” It is unclear how seriously the city and HRCS are considering the possibility. City spokesperson Scott Bean said “it’s one of the options on the table” the city is looking at, but “we would really like to get up and running sooner than 2028.” According to Bean, the initial $1.9 million set aside for site preparation and construction is no longer accurate. Moving the site to the county building’s west side parking lot ratcheted up the price tag, and final cost estimates are being evaluated. When asked whether the city had sufficiently provided progress checks to the public, Bean said it was “subjective.” “It’s tough because a lot of stuff is happening behind the scenes,” he said. “It’s hard to put out a public update about, ‘Hey, we had a meeting with the construction team to go through utility plans.’” In terms of tangible next steps, Bean said the city is “still just working with the construction partners at this point.” Lansing City Council President Peter Spadafore was unreachable for comment about the council’s response to the delays. The push for a comprehensive plan City officials are facing mounting backlash from advocates for the unhoused as the city continues to crack down on homeless encampments. Advocates are demanding actionable solutions–recent killings and approaching winter weather make living on the street dangerous–but have yet to see any long-term or permanent proposals from the city come to fruition. During a city council meeting on Monday, councilmember Nevarez Martinez opened with a biting statement condemning the city’s response, or lack thereof, to the demand for effective transitional and affordable housing for those experiencing homelessness. “I have grown increasingly frustrated by our city’s lack of a comprehensive homelessness strategy,” she said. “[The Nov. 9 city council] meeting made something painfully clear to me … we do not have a plan.” Nevarez Martinez proposed an emergency ordinance putting a 60-day moratorium on encampment sweeps and allowing encampments in select city parks. She also proposed an ad hoc committee to craft a strategy. The number of residents who spoke in support of, and against, taking up the ordinance and establishing the committee during t

articles.description: Jason and Lucia's crime-heavy love story fuels a wonder of digital urban simulation.
articles.content: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers.Read full article Comments

articles.title: A $2.2B RenCen makeover. Are Detroiters getting enough in return?
articles.description: Detroit City Council postponed action Tuesday on a set of proposals tied to the Detroit Renaissance Center redevelopment plan. Here's why.
articles.content: Detroit’s City Council delayed action Tuesday on the proposed $2.2 billion makeover of the Renaissance Center and East Riverfront as members and residents continue to press developers on unanswered questions and improved benefits like more job guarantees, public ownership of land next to the towers, and more. City Council President James Tate announced the panel’s intention to postpone votes on the package of vital tax incentives and proposed community benefits at the top of the packed meeting.Still, much of public comment was dominated by residents, advocates, newly elected State Rep. Chris Gilmer-Hill of Michigan’s 8th House District and two Detroit Police Commissioners weighing in on the redevelopment.Here are the highlights:COMMUNITY QUESTIONS, COMMENTS, CONCERNS? Scenes from the Detroit City Council formal session on November, 17, 2026. Credit: City of Detroit Flickr The 100-plus public commenters ran a gamut of familiar celebrations, concerns, questions and critiques. Support for the project was mostly voiced by development, union and construction interests. Other supporters spoke about the proposed economic benefits of the project for residents and working Detroiters, as well as the positive legacy it could leave future generations. The people pushing back continue to argue for more concrete and enforceable promises from developers that would bring direct benefits to Detroiters. This includes solid plans for things like the marina, maintaining the remaining affordable living downtown and environmental concerns tied to the deconstruction of two of the five RenCen towers. Most called on council members to delay voting, or at least to “delay and improve” the community benefits agreement. Folks from both sides were grateful for the delay, and had critiques about how fast the community benefits process has been and that it’s already in front of the full council for consideration. During a Monday community meeting about the project hosted by Council Member Mary Waters there was a more firm and specific public ownership demand from organizers with Detroit People’s Platform. They are asking the development team to donate 18 acres of land next to the RenCen to the city and an endowment to help pay for maintenance and upkeep. The developers have referred to the land as “civic space,” which is committed to be accessible. However, advocates say there’s uncertainty over what would happen with this space after the tax abatement being sought for the project ends. Between Waters’ Monday meeting and Tuesday’s council session, there were also concerns about transparency and accountability, especially when it came to a confidential Law Department memo on community ownership. WHERE DO THE COUNCIL MEMBERS STAND?While there is technically no deadline for council to vote, developers have spoken about their urgency in advancing the deal so they can secure state-level approvals from the Michigan Strategic Fund. Bedrock representative Steve Ogden implied Monday that part of the developers’ urgency stems from wanting to get the local approvals before Democratic Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson takes office in January. Ogden said both Benson and her former opponent, Republican John James, “are on record saying they want to blow up” the Michigan Economic Development Corporation, the public-private partnership crated to carry out MSF programs. Ogden said potential MEDC changes could result in delays for the development timeline. Detroit City Council Member Mary Waters said she wants more benefits for businesses to be considered as part of the RenCen deal. Credit: City of Detroit Flickr President Pro Tem Coleman A. Young II, who recently touted the public benefits of the project, told BridgeDetroit after Tuesday’s meeting he was ready to vote ‘yes’ on the RenCen proposals, and expected votes as soon as next week. Meanwhile, Council Member Gabriela Santiago-Romeromaintained her position of bringing the measures back in the new year. Tate and Council Members Angela Whitfield-Calloway and Scott Benson were largely focused on getting questions answered, and letting those answers and community input to shape their votes. Along with other council members, the three received answers to memos on a variety of issues like East Riverfront ownership, Gilbert’s $1 billion nonprofit which would manage and own the redevelopment, the proposed abatement structures (like payments-in-lieu-of-taxes) developers are seeking and more. Waters on Monday echoed similar sentiments and said that she wanted to work with developers, especially on potentially increasing benefits for businesses. “Now I get my opportunity to say to Bedrock, ‘Okay, but can we do A? Can we do B? Can we do C?’ Just to kind of help pump up the benefits and put some of our residents at ease,” Waters said. “To let folks know that we care, we hear you, we see you.” Representatives for council members Renata Miller and Latisha Johnson declined comment on their behalf after Tuesday’s meeting. Council Member Denzell McCampbell could not be reached Tuesday evening. WHAT HAPPENS NOW AND HOW CAN I BE INVOLVED? There are two key meetings for this issue remaining before the council goes on winter recess starting Nov. 25. → Thursday’s Planning and Economic Development subcommittee is slated to feature remaining and new memos from council members. You can attend at 10 a.m. at the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center, or virtually here. articles.title: Own a large building in Detroit? The city wants to know your energy usage.
articles.description: In Detroit, 22% of applicable buildings are compliant with an ordinance passed in 2023 requiring water and energy usage reports.
articles.content: Detroit is slowly making progress on tracking the energy and water use of thousands of buildings across the city. Currently one-fifth of 2,500 buildings in Detroit have met the reporting requirements of a 2023 ordinance spearheaded by the city’s Green Taskforce designed to audit conditions that contribute to climate change. It applies to buildings 25,000 square feet and up and requires owners to report annual energy and water use. The effort comes with free workshops and resources for building owners. Detroit has warmed more than four degrees Fahrenheit since 1970, contributing to more intense rainfall and extreme weather events, extreme heat that can be dangerous, and other effects on the ecosystems and humans. Residential and commercial buildings account for 40% of greenhouse gas emissions nationally that contribute to this climate warming, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute. In Detroit, the number is even higher: 63%. Notices were mailed out to all business owners with qualifying buildings, said city senior energy analyst, Zahra Seblini, who administers the ordinance. And the city, in partnership with Detroit 2030 District, and the Midwest Energy Efficiency Alliance have hosted more than 50 workshops to get people oriented to the ordinance Roughly 550 out of 2,500 buildings are compliant with the ordinance according to the city’s Office of Sustainability. Building owners who have not yet submitted their data through the Environmental Protection Agency’s energy manager system have until 2028 to do so before the city will begin issuing blight tickets for not meeting the requirements of the ordinance. Seblini said the goal isn’t to issue a ticket though. “The whole point of the law is to get building owners excited about energy and water tracking and decarbonization as an option for them,” she said. “A lot of business owners don’t even consider it as an option, they think they’re at the will of rising energy costs.” Every year, Michigan utilities request and are granted increases on their energy rates. Michigan pays the most per kilowatt hour out of Midwest states. More than 50 cities across the United States have similar ordinances. It’s common to take several years to reach majority compliance, said Seblini. It took Ann Arbor four years to reach 50% compliance, said Connor Dailey, energy analyst for the City of Ann Arbor, which passed its benchmarking ordinance in 2021. Lee Visci, board president for the Great Lakes Tower Condos in Harbortown on the Detroit River, said reporting for the ordinance was “rocky” when she first reported it several years ago, because every bill had to be manually entered. But now the system has been updated to automatically sync utility bills and requires no work on Visci’s part to annually report the data. Since the ordinance passed, the city has hosted 10-15 in-person events each year to help building owners with the ordinance. “We invite people to bring their laptops, we introduce them to the ordinance, introduce them to the city’s overall climate strategy, and then we share their role in the city’s approach to climate change and resiliency,” said Seblini. Under the ordinance, buildings are only required to report their usage, not reduce it. Visci questioned “the end game.” But just tracking a building’s energy reduces usage by 7%, according to the American Cities Climate Challenge. Tracking is a precondition for energy efficiency projects, awards, and grants from the city, added Seblini. The city plans to get 100% of its electricity from clean energy by 2034. Visci said she’s looking forward to seeing how much energy other buildings of similar size use. “What I’m hoping to see is the benefit of sharing the benchmarking data and lessons learned, so that we can all kind of be more responsible energy stewards going forward,” she said. Seblini said it’s “a possibility” for the future to share other buildings’ usage, but that data is anonymized right now. In the meantime, the private-public partnership Detroit 2030 District, has free resources including education, building audits, and access to groups organized by building type for sharing best practices. Already the ordinance has allowed the city to “reach building owners and direct information about the city’s goals and opportunities for energy efficiency and decarbonization, and other resources for recycling, composting, indoor air quality and resilience,” said Seblini. The information will also help the city build its citywide decarbonization strategy, added Seblini. A map showing buildings in compliance is publicly available online.

Rogers continues push for environmental literacy framework, reconnecting students with the outdoors
articles.description: As the Michigan Legislature heads into its lame duck session following the Nov. 3 election, a Kalamazoo Democrat is renewing her push to improve education on environmental issues. Last week, state Rep. Julie Rogers introduced House Bill 6465, which would establish a 13-member task force to adopt an environmental literacy pathway for students from prekindergarten […]
articles.content: State Rep. Julie M. Rogers (D-Kalamazoo) in 2025. (Michigan House Democrats photo)As the Michigan Legislature heads into its lame duck session following the Nov. 3 election, a Kalamazoo Democrat is renewing her push to improve education on environmental issues. Last week, state Rep. Julie Rogers introduced House Bill 6465, which would establish a 13-member task force to adopt an environmental literacy pathway for students from prekindergarten through 12th grade. This framework is intended to prepare students to understand and address environmental issues in their community, contribute to healthy lifestyles by making outdoor experiences a regular part of school curriculum, and teach students about jobs in fields like alternative energy, renewable fuels and materials science that can help protect the environment. The framework also includes education about equity, disproportionate impacts, cumulative impacts and the unique needs of individual communities facing environmental challenges. Speaking with Michigan Advance, Rogers, who was elected to the state Senate on Nov. 3, said she’d been working on the bill for quite a while, introducing a previous version in 2023. “My sister is a educator, and she had had several other educators talk to her about climate change and also the fact that we have so many youth facing mental health issues with screen time and not really getting outdoors,” Rogers said. She stressed that her proposal was not a mandate for teachers, but a framework for teaching environmental literacy, allowing districts to decide whether they’d like to opt in. Climate literacy in crisis: Why understanding climate science matters now more than ever “My kind of vision is to have several touch points throughout K through 12,” Rogers said. “In Julie’s perfect world, it would be a touch point in elementary school, a touch point in middle school and another time in high school. And this would not be a separate class. It would be designed to embed with current existing curricula to weave in some of this information.” In addition to the environmental literacy pathway, the bill instructs the task force to develop a guidance document to identify professional development opportunities for teachers, explain how to implement their environmental literacy pathway, and showcase ways to encourage educational agencies and schools to participate in programs that support environmental education. Between the initial version introduced in 2023 and the recently-reintroduced policy, Rogers has added some stipulations on the makeup of the task force. In the most recent version, one member of the task force must be from an urban school district, while another must be from a rural school district. “One of the things that’s no secret is in some of the more urban, heavy industry areas of Michigan, there’s been quite a bit of air quality issues and environmental justice impacts….And then Michigan has such a rich agricultural history with many farms, and they sometimes have their own set of environmental challenges,” Rogers said when asked how these differing perspectives could enrich the task force’s conversation around local environmental impacts. The task force would also include a seat for a student appointed by the state superintendent, who would act as an advisor rather than a voting member. Rogers pointed to Michigan Youth Leaders For Environmental Stewardship, as among the bill’s supporters, later reflecting on testimony during a 2023 committee hearing for the bill where a student activist discussed the anxiety that can arise when students are not educated about climate change and its solutions. Alongside helping students build a personal relationship with their environment, Rogers said she also hoped to expose students to different career pathways, pointing to the state’s 2023 clean energy policy, which aims to shift Michigan’s grid to a 100% clean energy standard by 2040. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “I think over the next eight to 10 years, we’re going to see Michigan’s energy sector transformed, and we are going to need students trained to go into those fields, whether it be wind or solar,” Rogers said. “I just think as we’re diversifying our energy portfolio in Michigan, there’s going to be a whole new range of jobs to fill, and so it’s never too early, in my opinion, to start exposing students to those fields and career paths.” While speaking with youth activists about their concerns, climate-related tragedies like the record flooding the state experienced earlier this year was a key concern, Rogers said. “With that brings major devastation. It’s also very expensive, and then the state has to step in, or sometimes even the federal government,” Rogers said, noting that the activists she spoke with were passionate about taking a forward-thinking approach rather than simply reacting to these disasters. Serving on her county’s brownfield redevelopment commission for more than 10 years, Rogers said she’s been in the position of reacting to environmental messes. Now, she says it’s exciting to be in a leadership position where she can work to try and mitigate environmental harm through education. While the Michigan House is controlled by a 58-52 Republican majority, Democrats were able to win control of the chamber this past election. With Democrats retaining control of the Senate and current Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson winning the governor’s seat, a Democratic trifecta will control the executive seat and both chambers of the state legislature. With little over a month and limited session days remaining on the House’s schedule, the clock is ticking for lawmakers to take action on Rogers’ bill. If the year comes to an end without any movement, Rogers said she plans to reintroduce the policy in the state Senate, where she’ll take office in the coming year.

articles.description: The Trump administration has made a flurry of changes to the rules that govern international students. Advocates say it’s an intentional attack.
articles.content: (Etai Smotrich-Barr / Michigan Public)Shin, a flutist, was two years into a PhD in music at Michigan State University when he won an audition to join a nearby professional orchestra. Then, a few months later, he won another seat, this time in a major Michigan orchestra.“It felt like, ‘Oh, it’s happening, finally,'” Shin remembered. “I've been playing for so long and it's, I finally feel like I can actually make a living out of just playing.”Shin is an international student from Brazil. (Michigan Public is not using his full name because he is concerned that an interview could jeopardize his visa.)He was authorized to work in the U.S. through a program known as Curricular Practical Training (CPT), which lets international students participate in experiential learning opportunities that are directly related to the student’s area of study and “integral” to their degree.For the last 35 years, the Department of Homeland Security has interpreted that to include opportunities—like Shin’s orchestra membership—that were voluntary but directly linked to a specific course on the student’s schedule. But in August, just before the start of school, DHS issued new guidance: colleges and universities could only authorize CPT if “its absence would make the attainment of a degree an impossibility.”Most degree programs don’t mandate that students get an outside job. In effect, the new policy shut down the main pathway for international students to work off campus.Shin could find a new job on campus, but he couldn’t perform with the orchestras.“The first two weeks after that email, I couldn't close my eyes for more than two hours at a time,” Shin said. “I kept waking up and thinking, what am I going to do with my life now?”The Trump administration’s restrictions on CPT are only the latest in a flurry of changes to the regulations that govern international enrollment at U.S. universities — changes that advocates describe as an intentional attack.“What we have seen is an escalating cascade of policy actions and proposals, with the goal to really disrupt and dismantle the international student pipeline into the U.S.,” said Miriam Feldblum, President and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, an advocacy group composed of college and university leaders.In the last two years, Feldblum said, the Trump administration has: implemented a travel ban to 40 countries; delayed the visa review process and increased scrutiny of applicants’ social media; revoked students’ legal status without explanation; attempted to cap visas at four years, requiring students pursuing longer degrees, like PhDs, to apply for an extension midway through their program with no guarantee of approval; and attempted to charge tens of thousands of dollars in application fees for post-graduate work visas.Taken together, Feldblum said, these changes affect hundreds of thousands of international students in the U.S.“This is not about thoughtful, deliberate evaluation of what is working and what is not,” Feldblum said. “This is about wholesale disruption and dismantling of what we know makes the U.S. so great: that we are able to recruit and retain talent from around the world.”“And who's losing in this?” Feldblum added. “We're losing.”The Presidents’ Alliance is suing over some of these new policies, including the alterations to CPT. MSU filed a declaration supporting that lawsuit, which argues the Trump administration skipped due process when it bypassed the conventional rulemaking process to impose the new restrictions, essentially, overnight. (DHS framed the new CPT guidance as a “reminder” of existing obligations—despite evidence to the contrary—and threatened legal action for non-compliance.)DHS and the White House both declined an interview request. In a statement, a spokesperson for DHS wrote: “The performative outrage is incredible. Where was the outrage when foreign nationals were abusing the system, violating the terms of their student visas, and making a mockery of our immigration laws? If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege.”Administrators at a few Michigan universities told Michigan Public they’re doing their best to keep students up to date on all these changes: what’s proposed, in effect, or on hold in court. But they can only explain what the federal government tells them. In those conversations, administrators used one word again and again: “uncertainty.”'Before' and 'after' the second Trump administrationPasha, a PhD student at the University of Michigan from Islamabad, Pakistan, carries her immigration documents with her at all times. She keeps them in the front pocket of her overstuffed blue backpack. (“Pasha” is a nickname.)Non-citizens have long been required to carry proof of legal status, but the Trump administration has declared enforcement of that rule a priority.Pasha, who first entered the U.S. during the Biden administration, said she sees the requirement in a new light now: the documents she keeps within arm’s reach are a constant reminder that at any moment, she could be stopped by an immigration agent.“What would I say? If they're not listening to anyone, how would I tell them that I'm here legally and that I haven't done anything wrong? Would they believe me?” Pasha asked.She said her time in the United States has been split into a “before” and “after” the second Trump administration, “where at first I was just part of society, and now I'm someone who in this society needs to carry my papers to prove my identity.”Declining international enrollmentUniversities in Michigan, and across the U.S., have seen a decline in international enrollment over the last two years.This fall, Michigan’s nine R1 and R2 research universities enrolled 19% fewer international students compared to fall of 2024, according to Michigan Public’s analysis of university enrollment reports, amounting to a loss of more than 3,900 students. MSU has lost more than 600 international students in that span. At U-M, that number is just over 1,100.One reason for that decline could be increased global competition, according to Adem Althor, executive director of global engagement at Oakland University.Althor said that unlike ten years ago, when “international students would just kind of appear like manna from heaven,” the U.S. now has to contend with new players like Dubai and Singapore that operate increasingly compelling programs.But he also said prospective international students are expressing serious concern about “changes to the regulatory landscape” in the U.S.“Students are making a serious investment in their education and they want certainty just like any other investor would,” Althor said. “They want to know: what are the rules of the road for the next several years?”And, he added, “some countries are making that clearer than others."Feldblum, of the Presidents’ Alliance, said the Trump administration’s recent changes have made the U.S. a less attractive option for international students, “exactly when the global marketplace has become more competitive.”Put another way, Feldblum said, “We are shooting ourselves in the foot.”Why stay?On Tuesday, November 17, a federal district court issued a preliminary injunction that temporarily blocks the Trump administration’s changes to CPT. That means colleges and universities can approve students for off-campus work — at least until the court issues a final ruling.But the pause is coming too late to help Shin.In order to focus on performing with the orchestras, Shin had to leave an on-campus job as a teaching assistant. But this fall, he said, without either the orchestra roles or the teaching job, he realized he could no longer afford spring tuition. He’s set to graduate in December—just a few weeks from now—and has been rushing to finish his dissertation.At Michigan State, Shin had been trying to live by a philosophy passed down from his dad: “leave a good mark wherever you go.” But over the last few months, he said, he’s realized the U.S. might not want him to contribute anything beyond tuition dollars.If the Trump administration is trying to discourage international students from coming to the U.S., at least according to Shin, it’s working.“Wherever I want to go, I want to make the place better,” Shin said. “And if that's not something that I can do here, then I don't want to be here anymore.”Even so, Shin said that after graduation, he's applying for a different, one-year work authorization program called Optional Practical Training (OPT), so that he can perform with the Michigan orchestras for at least one more season before he goes back to Brazil.But he needs to get approved quickly, before another policy change takes effect: the Trump administration recently proposed a $70,000 application fee for OPT.If that happens, Shin said, he’s going home.

Lansing can do better than a tent in a park
articles.description: Fifteen years ago, then-Mayor Virg Bernero wrapped himself in the “Occupy Wall Street” movement by allowing protesters to “occupy Lansing” by sleeping overnight at Reutter Park, across Capitol Avenue from […]
articles.content: Fifteen years ago, then-Mayor Virg Bernero wrapped himself in the “Occupy Wall Street” movement by allowing protesters to “occupy Lansing” by sleeping overnight at Reutter Park, across Capitol Avenue from the library. Bernero, coming off an unsuccessful gubernatorial run, saw political mileage in latching onto a national movement about financial inequality. The “1%” own everything and the rest of us, the “99%” are doing our best to make do the best we can. Ingham County Judge Rosemarie Aquilina touring the Fallen Angels encampment in late 2025. Photo by Raymond Holt for City Pulse From October and into the winter, Bernero let protesters slowly turn Reutter Park into a collection of tents and tarps that looked more like a homeless encampment than an organized protest. Ultimately, the unsightly health and fire hazard got too much. The liability of passively letting someone potentially freeze to death by sleeping under the stars in a Lansing park drove Bernero to end the continuous sleepovers. By early December, the city had spent $20,000 over the two months of “occupation” to provide sanitation, trash pickup and public services to the park. Fast-forward to last year when Judge Rosemarie Aquilina toured the largest homeless encampment I’ve ever seen, behind Piazzano’s restaurant off Grand River Avenue. The judge spent more than an hour talking to residents, several of whom had been living in the woods beside the Grand River for more than two years. Appalled by it all, the judge ordered the city to move the people to what ended up being the Causeway Bay hotel. From there, many of them were offered services and a road to self-sufficiency. When I poked my head into this old property two weeks ago, it appeared the encampment had been long abandoned. And finally, it’s only been a few months since the most recent person had their face smashed in, potentially from a serial killer police suspect may be targeting unhoused men in the middle of the night. As a frequent River Trail user myself, I haven’t seen a collection of homeless people living along the trail in months. With these past events as a backdrop, it’s not hard to see why Lansing City Councilmember Deyanira Nevarez Martinez’s recent proposal to open select city parks from dusk to dawn for 60 days isn’t the solution. There’s the cost, the community aesthetics, the lack of facilities, the threat of open fires – all of the same issues that came with the “Occupy” encampments. Wrapping our arms around finding acceptable places for people to sleep outdoors in the winter, by extension, means we find it acceptable that people sleep outdoors in the winter. Judge Aquilina reminded us all last year that it was not. And let’s not forget, WE STILL HAVEN’T FOUND THE SERIAL KILLER OF HOMELESS MEN! Is it a stretch to think this person would find a way into one of these proposed parks, nearly all of which are in neighborhoods? Opening parks to camping, for any length of time, is a hard no. What her proposal does is spur city leaders, and really all of us, into action. It forces us to find and fund solutions that appeal to our humanity and sense of decency. Clearly, the city can be prodded into action when forced, as Judge Aquilina proved. The solution isn’t a winter encampment at Willoughby Park or on the River Trail underneath the Kalamazoo Street Bridge. It starts with a plan crafted by experts on how to transition the unhoused to more stable accommodations. Can we get a rough count of Lansing’s homeless population? Where are there available beds? Heated indoor accommodations with facilities? Are there enough service providers to pull it off? From there, city leaders need to put their stamp on it, city workers to make it happen, and for all of us to be fine paying for the solution with our tax dollars. Of course, we’re not the only community with a homeless population. Some may be concerned that any services we provide will draw more unhoused people to our community. The more we provide, the more folks will take advantage of the services. That’s one way to look at it. Another way is that by showing the rest of Michigan a model policy that’s funded by the public, other communities will have the courage to follow suit.
